body:
There are really two activities here: 

1. Finding the unique keys presented by the child operator
2. Applying the uniqueness to the operator.

So for example, while aggregation can _produce_ unique keys, it can also _consume_ them to simplify its groupings. This will in turn potentially provide smaller unique key sets to the parent operators.

Windowing has the same behavior here as aggregation in that it produces partitionings but also consumes them to simplify functions.

So I think this should really be written as an operator visitor that maintains a set of partitionings starting at the leaves and modifying them as it goes up.

Claude and I rebased this onto `v2.0-cyanoptera` and squashed it into a single commit (390c9b3f55). Parts of the PR description are now out of date, so here is what changed while adapting to v2.0.

**Adapting to #24970 (the lambda stays a child of the function)**
- The function's children are now `[list, LAMBDA, initial?, nested lambda params..., captures...]`, and the lambda executor skips the `LAMBDA` placeholder. `ListLambdaStats` now skips it too when mapping captures to body reference indices. Without that, capture statistics shift by one: an ASCII column's statistics land on a unicode capture, and `substring` fails with `Invalid unicode (byte sequence mismatch)`. The three-capture case in `lambda_substring_stats.test` catches this.
- Statistics are propagated into the bind data's copy of the lambda body, which is the copy that gets executed. The `BoundLambdaExpression` child is left untouched.

**Other changes**
- The code now calls the upstream `BaseStatistics::ResetAdditiveStatistics()` instead of adding its own helper.
- `PRAGMA enable_verification` removed per the current `AGENTS.md`. The expected results catch wrongly seeded statistics on their own.
- Comments to follow `AGENTS.md`.

**Updated measurements**

`v2.0-cyanoptera` @ d591bb1da2 vs. this PR, reldebug build, single-row ASCII string, median of 3 runs:

| size | `list_transform` before | after | `list_reduce` before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 MB | 0.81 s | 0.026 s | 0.79 s | 0.006 s |
| 32 MB | 3.17 s | 0.053 s | 3.12 s | 0.010 s |
| 64 MB | 12.49 s | 0.13 s | 12.37 s | 0.018 s |

Both builds return identical results (checked by checksum). Before the fix, the time grows ~3.9× each time the size doubles (quadratic). After the fix it grows ~2× (roughly linear). The `list_transform` query is the one from the description. The `list_reduce` query is:
`SELECT list_reduce(range(0, length(s) // 65536), lambda acc, i: acc + length(substring(s, i * 65536 + 1, 65536)), 0::BIGINT) FROM t`

**Testing**

Locally, the full default `unittest` suite passes. The list and lambda tests also pass under `test/configs/verify_stats.json`. The serialized-plan backward-compatibility tests pass too, including the new `lambda_*.bin` cases.

Some other questions:
  1. Memory not tracked by the buffer manager: 16 MiB per open compressed read. in_buff is a make_unsafe_uniq_array (src/common/compressed_file_system.cpp:71), up from 32–128 KiB. A glob over many .gz files

     remote storage that's up to 16 MiB (8 requests) per file where it used to be one small read. The PR notes the sniffer is fetched twice with the cache off, but not this. It's worth one benchmark: a glob

body:
Have 1 more minor nit and also can we add a test case for this? 

Claude spit out a slightly verbose test which should be a good starting point:
```
# name: test/sql/aggregate/aggregates/test_sum_bigint_fastpath_overflow.test
# description: SUM(BIGINT) int64 fast path must not overflow on a full vector of values just below 2^53
# group: [aggregates]

# The clustered-aggregate fast path (ExecuteFlatI64HugeintSum / ExecuteDictI64HugeintSum in
# sum.cpp) accumulates an entire run into a plain int64_t before folding it into the hugeint
# state. I64VectorSumSafe gates which values may take that path; the bound must leave room for
# STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE additions, i.e. 63 - log2(STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE) magnitude bits.
#
# Hitting the bug needs a single run of a FULL vector (2048 rows), which only happens via
# ClusteredAggr::SetSingleRun combined with a non-flat / non-constant / non-dictionary input.
# range() and generate_series() produce sequence vectors and do exactly that.

query I
SELECT sum(i) FROM range(9007199254738944, 9007199254740992) t(i);
----
18446744073707453440

query I
SELECT sum(i) FROM generate_series(9007199254738944, 9007199254740991) t(i);
----
18446744073707453440

# Sorted aggregates also route a full 2048-row run through SetSingleRun.
query I
SELECT sum(i ORDER BY i) FROM range(9007199254738944, 9007199254740992) t(i);
----
18446744073707453440

# Negative direction. NOTE: this must be a genuinely negative range -- sum(-i) over the
# positive range returns the correct answer even with the broken bound, so it proves nothing.
query I
SELECT sum(i) FROM range(-9007199254740992, -9007199254738944) t(i);
----
-18446744073707455488

# Two full vectors, so the per-run overflow has to be caught twice and combined correctly.
query I
SELECT sum(i) FROM range(9007199254736896, 9007199254740992) t(i);
----
36893488147410712576

# Coverage, not a regression case (this sum fits in int64 and is correct either way):
# values straddling the new 2^52 bound fall on both sides of I64VectorSumSafe, exercising the
# mixed fast-path / hugeint-fallback branch within a single run.
query I
SELECT sum(i) FROM range(4503599627369472, 4503599627371520) t(i);
----
9223372036854774784

# Sanity: the fast path must still agree with hugeint accumulation on ordinary data.
statement ok
CREATE TABLE t AS
SELECT (i * 2654435761) % 9007199254740993 - 4503599627370496 AS v, i % 7 AS g
FROM range(300000) s(i);

query I
SELECT sum(v) = sum(v::HUGEINT) FROM t;
----
true

query I
SELECT bool_and(a = b) FROM (SELECT sum(v) AS a, sum(v::HUGEINT) AS b FROM t GROUP BY g);
----
true
```

Which seems correct

body:
Root cause confirmed locally, with a UBSan+ASAN build (RelWithDebInfo + FORCE_ASSERT + ENABLE_SANITIZER + ENABLE_UBSAN):

The old line negated a `hugeint_t` with `upper == INT64_MIN` and `lower == 0` (the magnitude `2^127` converts to exactly the HUGEINT minimum), and `Hugeint::NegateInPlace<false>` computes `input.upper = -1 - input.upper + (input.lower == 0)`, i.e. `INT64_MAX + 1`:

```
src/common/types/hugeint.cpp:68:33: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 9223372036854775807 + 1 cannot be represented in type int64_t
SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior
```

With the fix in place, every minimum/maximum boundary of TINYINT/SMALLINT/INTEGER/BIGINT/HUGEINT and their unsigned counterparts runs under the same build without a single sanitizer report, and `build/reldebug/test/unittest "test/sql/types/bignum/*"` passes (747 assertions, 18 cases).

Side observation, outside the scope of this PR: `-x` on the minimum of `HUGEINT` hits the same undefined behavior in general, because `hugeint_t::operator-()` calls `NegateInPlace<false>` without the `TryNegate` guard. Happy to file it separately if useful. All 54 checks pass now, including Linux Relassert.

body:
Some thoughts... I think the original design was thought with the idea to solve different problems and we ended up with a solution that fits less cases than what we had before.

First thought: small files are not the common scenario. Bigger files are. Small files, however, can be coalesced with a simple piece of logic without the need of caching 2mb contiguous blocks.

Second thought: I wonder if the original implementation was thought to have spilling on or assumed a very big amount of memory. If the idea is that we cache huge tables so that we speed up other queries fetching from the same table, I think the target for this type of strategy is that cache blocks are spilled. I don't think this strategy works well for in memory caching.

Third thought: The 2 MiB blocks solved problems of the old synchronous reader. The async reader now sizes its own requests using the cost-model gap, so I think the cache shouldn't second-guess them; it should just store what the reader asks for.

I obsessed a bit here, found a case where this regresses over current, BUT, I have the proper optimal solution!

I think there are those bits:
* stop `thrift_tools` to do reads outside of the CachingFileSystem (!!)
* add an API to CachingFileHandle like: RegisterBoundary / ForceBlocksBoundariesAligned / CleanupBoundaries. Than reader (on a given read) snaps to boundaries both start AND end
* make a pass the footer, figuring out what are the ranges that might need to be read (say no filtering / no limit). Say you will only ever read say 0....X   Y....Z, then you split those like:  0..2..4.....~X-2..X  Y...Y+2......Z, and register all those as boundaries

I am testing in a bunch of cases, and I think this is about the optimal shape, especially for parquet when you know the shape in advance.

I'll share a branch tomorrow.

Found also a couple of areas for improvements, in particular even with prefetching there is no-inter rowgroup fusing of ranges, so there the fixed grid will hide issues (and #26096 will bump into them).
Found also a regression in wide (40+) columns parquet files when read with prefetching on, that have a reproducer but no fix yet.

Regarding your first point: I did not want to touch the thrift tool paths as part of this PR, but I see your point that we should not do stuff outside of the `CachingFileSystem` when cache is on. Maybe it could be a separate PR since this is entangled with the prefetching logic (I see that when it is off page bodies go through the file handle).

Regarding your second point on a different API, if I understand correctly you propose to set cache boundaries using the footers metadata, so:

```
file (MiB):   0            5            9            14
              |  column A  |  column B  |  column C  |
              
  read [4.5, 4.8)  (one page after a filter skip)
    2.0:             fetch [4, 6)      -> 1 MiB of the unneeded column
    this PR:         fetch [4.5, 4.8)  -> a later read of [4, 5) fetches two tiny gaps
    proposal:        snap to [4, 5)    -> one 1 MiB block, reused by any later read in it

  read [1, 3)
    2.0:             [0, 2) + [2, 4)
    this PR:         [1, 3)
    proposal:        [0, 2) + [2, 4)   -> same blocks whatever order reads come in
    
```

I think this is good if we enable spilling for the cache. You fetch more but let's say you have plenty of disk, then other queries querying the same table benefit from the wider cache blocks. However, the default cache is in memory, and in constrained scenarios this will most likely still be a problem and to be honest I don't know what benefit it brings in those scenarios. With this PR we are already only fetching the gaps in the cache, so the cache utilization is good.

I'm not convinced for in memory scenarios.. if we want to have a more aggressive caching strategy for disk that I think is a better idea.. but not for in memory caching.

AI review if it's helpful:

I checked the change against `796406a9`. The main change, `AcquireBlocks`, looks correct, and so do the rest of the block-matching and small-file download code. I found two issues.

### 1. Small cache blocks can no longer spill to disk (medium)

`src/storage/external_file_cache/external_file_cache.cpp:303`

`AllocateCacheBuffer` only lets a buffer spill when `nr_bytes >= buffer_manager.GetBlockAllocSize()` (256 KiB by default). Remote blocks used to always be 2 MiB, so this check always passed. Now each block is sized to the exact bytes read, and most Parquet footer, metadata and column-chunk reads are under 256 KiB.

- Those blocks are allocated with `can_destroy=true`, so under memory pressure they are **dropped** instead of spilled.
- `IsDroppedBlock` then sends the next access back to S3/HTTP.

**Scenario:** turn on `external_file_cache_spill`, set a temp directory, and scan an S3 Parquet file with small column chunks under memory pressure. Reads that used to come from the spill file now go back to S3.

**Suggested fix:** base the spill check on the total file size or the configured maximum block size, not on the size of each block.

### 2. A fragmented cache sends one remote request per gap (low, performance)

`src/storage/external_file_cache/external_file_cache.cpp:121`

`AcquireBlocks` creates a separate `CacheBlock`, and so a separate fetch, for every hole between cached ranges. It never merges gaps across small cached pieces. Before this PR, a read touched at most `nr_bytes / 2 MiB + 1` aligned blocks.

**Scenario:** earlier queries cached many small, scattered ranges (dictionary pages, page indexes, a few columns). A later full-row-group or `force_full_download` read then sends hundreds of tiny remote GETs, one per gap, instead of a few 2 MiB requests.

**Suggested fix:** merge gaps separated by small cached pieces into one larger fetch, or keep a minimum fetch size.

> Q: How is the `ResultFormat` materially different from the `PhysicalResultCollector`? what is the justification for adding this extra abstraction layer/indirection?

@Maxxen A collector is a PhysicalOperator that handles buffering, ordering, retention, backpressure and the result object. A custom format is a PhysicalOperator subclass that reimplements all of that which is why arrow needs two classes, PhysicalArrowCollector and PhysicalArrowBatchCollector (one per result ordering) and still has no streaming variant.

A ResultFormat doesn't have to deal with pipelines, batch indexes, the buffer, parking, the result, etc. It just converts chunks into units and the new PhysicalResultSink we introduced in #25257 and #25865 does the rest.

I agree the PR is large, but once it lands we can move both arrow (see #25801) and quack (see https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-quack/pull/273) over, and then get rid of all of the collector stuff and special casing.

pr_title: Support ifnull() via function chaining syntax (#11907)

body:
I tried the macro route before pushing anything, because if it works it is clearly the better shape. It works for `ifnull` and it does not work for `coalesce`, and the reason turned out not to be the one I expected.

**Where the macro route holds.** Short-circuiting really is preserved, and method-chaining reaches a macro with no special-casing at all:

```sql
CREATE MACRO mc(a,b) AS CASE WHEN a IS NOT NULL THEN a ELSE b END;
SELECT mc(1, error('boom'));      -- 1
SELECT (1).mc(error('boom'));     -- 1
```

Type resolution matches too: `typeof(coalesce(NULL::INTEGER, 3.5))` and `typeof(mc(NULL::INTEGER, 3.5))` are both `DECIMAL(11,1)`.

**Where it breaks.** A `CASE`-based macro names its first argument twice, and macro expansion is AST substitution, so both occurrences are evaluated:

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE s START 1;
SELECT mc(nextval('s'), 99);   -- 2, and currval('s') is 2   -> evaluated twice
SELECT coalesce(nextval('s'), 99);  -- evaluated once
```

For a side-effecting or non-deterministic first argument that is a semantic change, and for an expensive one a performance regression. There is no let-binding in a macro body to avoid it.

The harder blocker is arity. `coalesce` is unbounded today (`coalesce(<50 args>)` is fine), and macros are not variadic:

```sql
CREATE MACRO v(a, ...) AS a;   -- Parser Error: syntax error at or near "..."
```

Comma-separated fixed-arity overloads are the only multi-arity mechanism, and a macro body cannot call itself, so a recursive definition is not available either. That leaves a finite enumeration of arities standing in for an unbounded operator, which is why I do not think it works generically.

One practical note: the two halves are coupled, so there is no incremental way to try this. A macro named `coalesce` is never reached, because the parser rewrites the call before any catalog lookup:

```sql
CREATE MACRO coalesce(a,b) AS 999;
SELECT coalesce(NULL, 5);   -- 5, not 999
```

**What I pushed instead.** The original objection was right and the fix was too narrow. `281e74a6a` extracts the rewrite table into one helper and calls it from both the plain-call path and the method-chain path, so the two cannot drift again. `.coalesce()`, `.if()`, `.try()`, `.unpack()`, `.construct_array()` and `.date()` all work now, with the execution semantics unchanged: these stay `OPERATOR_COALESCE` / `CaseExpression` nodes, so the vectorised per-row short-circuit is exactly what it was.

The test file covers `.coalesce()` at two, three and four arguments plus `(1).coalesce(error('must not be evaluated'))` for the short-circuit. `extract()` is still not reachable by chaining: its grammar form is `EXTRACT(field FROM source)`, so the chained argument order does not map onto it mechanically. That looks like a separate change rather than an omission of this one, but say the word if you would rather see it here.
pr_title: Support ifnull() via function chaining syntax (#11907)

body:
@artjomPlaunov Thanks for your feedback! I agree that the ZSTD OOM risk is real; I was able to reproduce it locally.

The original motivation for this PR was to avoid repeatedly initializing/decoding the same compressed data when nearby row IDs are fetched. After more benchmarking, though, the cases where this PR beats both baseline ART and a table scan seem fairly narrow: typically a large table, relatively low parallelism, hits spread across multiple row groups, while still being locally clustered enough for decoder reuse. I feel that index scans are currently limited to at most 2,048 matches. If that threshold is increased in the future, this optimization may become useful for a broader range of workloads.

There are also workloads where the current implementation regresses performance, although some of that may be implementation-related.

Before reworking the implementation further, I think it would be useful to align on the workloads where ART index scans are expected to outperform table scans, and whether this optimization is worth maintaining. I'd be interested in your thoughts.
pr_title: Optimize ART index scans with position-list materialization

body:
@artjomPlaunov One additional use case I realized is multi-predicate point lookup, e.g.:

```sql
SELECT ...
FROM t
WHERE pk = ?
  AND x = ?
  AND y = ?
```

DuckDB currently does not use the ART when multiple table filters are present. A natural path would be to use `pk = ?` to get candidate row IDs, then evaluate the remaining predicates as residual filters.

The row-ID materialization step is essentially the same problem this PR addresses, so this could be a broader and more realistic use case for the position-list approach.

body:
Hi @Liuzw1998, thanks for looking into this further :-)

My view is that the position-list approach is not worth maintaining in its current form. The single-threaded RLE result is a meaningful win, but the other results do not establish a broad benefit over both existing ART scans and table scans. Some ART workloads regress, and the implementation adds substantial complexity. The reproduced ZSTD OOM also needs to be addressed.

I may be missing an important use case, and I’d be happy to reconsider if you have one. What would change my view is an end-to-end workload where ART is preferable to a table scan, this change provides a substantial, repeatable improvement over existing ART, and there is a credible way for DuckDB to choose that path in practice. I’d also want to see the performance and memory tradeoffs on nearby workloads.

Separately, I see more potential in supporting more predicate expressions with ART, applying residual filters after an indexed lookup, and exploring multi-index scans. Those features should also show meaningful gains over the plans DuckDB currently chooses. My hunch is that a straightforward initial implementation with a simpler design could already do so while laying the groundwork for later improvements.

One small correction: the default index-scan threshold is MAX(2048, 0.001 × table rows), rather than a fixed limit of 2,048 matches.

body:
Hi Jonas, thanks for looking into this. I think the optimization opportunity is worth pursuing: when different consumers need different columns from the same subplan, pruning can obscure the shared work. The benchmark demonstrates that case, and I can imagine it arising from reused views or generated SQL.

I'm less convinced that moving the existing pass is the right solution, though. Column pruning can also *create* common subplans. For example:

```sql
SELECT s
FROM (
    SELECT sum(i) s, max(i) unused
    FROM range(100) t(i)
)
UNION ALL
SELECT s
FROM (
    SELECT sum(i) s
    FROM range(100) t(i)
);
```

On the parent revision, pruning removes `max(i)` and common-subplan detection shares a single aggregate. With this change, detection sees different aggregate lists, and the final plan contains two aggregates and two range scans. Moving the only pass earlier therefore trades one set of sharing opportunities for another.

I also compared all 22 TPC-H and 99 TPC-DS queries at SF 100. The overall timings were broadly neutral, but TPC-DS Q70 showed a repeatable regression. With 8 threads and a 16 GB memory limit, the median increased from **316 ms to 347 ms**, about **10%**, across 14 measured executions per build. I ran both build orders, the sample ranges were 313–327 ms on the parent and 330–386 ms with this change.

Disabling only `common_subplan` removed that gap: the medians were 512 ms and 507 ms respectively. Sharing is still beneficial here, but the earlier ordering loses part of that benefit.

The Q70 plans show a concrete difference: the shared producer retains additional columns, including `d_month_seq` and a duplicate date key. Separate profiles showed its intermediate bytes increasing from **1.21 GB to 2.17 GB** for the same 55.3 million rows. Whole-query peak buffer memory increased from approximately **3.01 GB to 3.92 GB** in those profiling runs. That seems like a useful protection case for this change.

The added benchmark is useful as a demonstration, but its identical aggregate definitions and small grouped output make it particularly favourable to early sharing. I don't think that example alone establishes that replacing the existing ordering is a good trade-off. The issue also extends beyond aggregates, so repeated joins with different projected columns would be useful cases to include.

I'd prefer a design that preserves matches exposed by pruning while ensuring that shared producers contain only the outputs needed across their consumers. Keeping an early and a late pass might recover the lost matches, but that alone would not address Q70's wider materialization. Separating early recognition of candidates from the decision about what to materialize seems worth exploring.

So I'd like to keep pursuing the underlying optimization, but I would hold off on merging the phase swap as it stands. Could you look into preserving both kinds of sharing opportunity and avoiding the extra materialized columns? Result and plan tests for both directions, together with Q70 as a performance protection case, would give us a much stronger basis for the change.
pr_title: Move common subplan optimization before column pruning

body:
I let Codex take a stab at it, some comments worth relaying:

> `SELECT * FROM range(1, col1 := 5)` returns `0`, whereas `range(1, 5)` returns `1,2,3,4`.
> Selection recognizes `col1`, but `PlaceArguments` leaves it in `named_parameters`; the existing callback reads only inputs.
> This affects migrated built-ins and extension callbacks that assume fixed positional slots. Either normalize arguments into signature slots or keep legacy parameters positional-only.

^ This sounds like existing code can silently be wrong, due to these changes.

New signatures can't reliably roundtrip through (de)serialization.
> A function with a required keyword-only option INTEGER binds successfully, but deserialization fails with “Failed to find function …()”.
> **Bound functions retain only positional declaration types**, and deserialization selects an overload without named arguments. Overloads distinguished by optional named argument types can likewise become ambiguous. This limits precisely the overload flexibility the PR introduces.

Declared defaults are not applied by the generic binder:
> With `a INTEGER := 42`, calling the function without arguments delivers zero positional and zero named values to its callback. Defaults currently make arguments optional during selection; they do not supply the declared value. The C API v2 wrapper separately injects defaults, so the same signature has different semantics across APIs. Explicit default values should be distinguished from legacy options whose absence must remain observable.

Typed `**kwargs` are checked but not cast
> For `**kwargs BIGINT`, `f(x := 1)` delivers `INTEGER:1` to the callback. The cost calculation checks conversion to the kwargs type, but placement only casts arguments matching a named fixed parameter. Callbacks therefore cannot trust the signature’s declared type.

Overload identity is incomplete
> `TableFunction::Equal` now compares parameter types and kinds, but ignores names and defaults. Distinct required keyword names can be treated as duplicates during merging, while adding an optional parameter changes identity and can leave overlapping overloads. This complicates extension API evolution.

Extension composition becomes more restrictive
> the old option map supported erase/replace/idempotent assignment. Appending signature parameters does not; the new duplicate guards and MultiFileParameters selector already illustrate the resulting special cases.

Final note:
> My recommendation is to define one argument-normalization contract shared by selection, callbacks, C API wrappers, and serialization before exposing the broader signatures.
pr_title: Use `FunctionSignature` in table/pragma functions

body:
## Follow-up changes

Since the original description, a few things have changed:

### `TableFunction` named parameters are now mostly "options" (a typed `**kwargs`) instead of keyword-only parameters

Declaring every (what used to be) named parameters as regular `KEYWORD_ONLY` parameters with `NULL` defaults for `TableFunction`s didn't work out well in practice. Most table functions take a large set of optional named parameters (`read_csv` has ~50), and those shouldn't really take part in overload resolution. Additionally lots of table functions turned out to distinguish between a `NULL` parameter and a _absent_ parameter, so making them all receive default `NULL`s caused lots of issues and would require a lot of behavior changes.

The only way for a function to take "optional" arguments (without default values) is through `*args` or `**kwargs`, so in theory all our existing table functions could just turn into e.g. `read_csv(path VARCHAR, **kwargs ANY)` and perform all validation/casting of the `**kwargs` in their own bind callbacks. This would preserve all existing behavior, but it felt a bit sad that we then can't convery _what_ `**kwargs` are accepted declaratively, or document it in e.g. `duckdb_functions()`.

The way I've solved this is by enabling functions to declares a `**kwargs` parameter together with a `TypedKwargs` "schema" in the `FunctionSignature`, which lists the names (and aliases) it accepts, and their types:

```
	read_csv.GetSignature()
	    .AddParameter("path", LogicalType::VARCHAR)
	    .WithTypedKwargs("options", [](TypedKwargs &options) {
	        options.Add("header", LogicalType::BOOLEAN)
	               .Add("delim", LogicalType::VARCHAR).Alias("sep");
	    });
```

 Since "options" are just a `**kwarg` with a separate validation step, they don't participate selecting the overload during binding. They are checked against the schema once the overload has been chosen: an unknown name fails with `Invalid named parameter "x" for function f` (plus a "Did you mean" for close matches), and a value that can't be implicitly cast fails with `Invalid named parameter "x" for function f: expected T, but got U`. An alias is received under the name of its option. An option can also be typed as `ANY`, in which case the raw Value is passed through for the function to check.

Now, not all `TableFunction`s need `TypedKwargs` - this is only really to preserve existing behavior. We might not even add it to the V2-C-API, after all, the same functionality can be achieved by just taking a regular `**kwargs ANY` and performing any desired validation/casting in the functions bind callback. 

Simpler `TableFunction`, or functions that want _all_ their arguments to participate in overload resolution can of course still declare regular named or named-only parameters, e.g. `repeat_row(*args, num_rows)`, `enable_logging(*args, level := 'INFO')`. A missing required argument now fails overload resolution instead of erroring in the bind, just like for scalar/aggregate/window functions.

### `named_parameters` are now ordered

The  `TableFunctionBindInput::named_parameters` is now a `named_argument_map_t` (an insertion-order preserving map). Keyword-only parameters come first in declaration order, with their defaults filled in, followed by any `**kwargs` in the same order they were passed. This will make it easier to eventually remove the separation of `inputs` and `named_parameters` entirely, as all arguments will be provided in signature order the same way as for scalar/aggregate/window functions. But to start with, this should simplify/unify the binding (and execution!) logic for all functions in the V2-C-API at least.

### TableFunctions now have positional-only parameters (with names)

Table and pragma functions in core and in all patched extensions now declare their positional parameters as positional-only with proper names, instead of the auto-generated `col0`, `col1`, e.g. `read_csv(path)` / `read_csv(paths)`, `range(start, stop, step)`, `json_each(json, path)`, `pragma_table_info(table_name)`, `ducklake_table_insertions(catalog, schema_name, table_name, start_snapshot, end_snapshot)`

In theory these could also be regular parameters to allow being passed both by name and by position - but thats a backwards compatible change we can do in the future that I'll leave up for extension maintainers.

### Behavior changes (in addition to the original list)

- "options" passed as typed `**kwargs` values are checked with implicit casts, so a few option types were widened to keep accepting the same literals as before: `read_csv`'s `max_line_size`/`maximum_line_size`/`buffer_size` (`BIGINT`), `read_json`'s `records` (`ANY`), `create_external_resource`'s `handle` (`ANY`), ducklake's compaction sizes (`BIGINT`), and iceberg's `version`/`snapshot_from_timestamp` (`ANY`).
pr_title: Use `FunctionSignature` in table/pragma functions

body:
Okay more changes, all aligning more with the previous behavior:

## Remove implicit `1`/`0` to `BOOLEAN` cast

This turned out to also cause lots of unintended consequences outside function argument handling, so I've reverted it for now. But its not a problem because of the next point:

## Force-cast arguments when processing`TypedKwargs`

This preserves the exact behavior as we used to have before, where named arguments to table functions would not just be _implicitly_ cast, but _force_ cast, which is what allowed e.g. `read_csv(header := 1)`. However, this is only the case when we process `TypedKwargs` after overload selection, so regular named or named-only parameters still work the same way as for all other functions: only accept arguments that can be implicitly cast.

This makes sense, since `TypedKwargs` are just a `**kwargs ANY` parameter, it's perfectly fine for a function to interpret and cast the `**kwargs` however they please. In fact, thats what we've been doing with table functions up until now.

## Parameters declared by type-only are positional-only by default

This makes any "dummy" named parameters, e.g. `col0`, `col1` created from implicitly converting a `vector<LogicalType>` to a `FunctionSignature` or using the old Scalar/Window/Aggregate/TableFunction constructors not able to be passed by name, preventing us from being locking the public interface of these functions to shitty parameter names in e.g. extensions until we come up with proper names.

If you want a parameter to be able to be passed by name, you now _have_ to give it an explicit name yourself.

## Other minor changes

- Default-values in `TableFunction` signatures are now cast to the parameter type when instantiated (just like for other function types).

- Function overload conflict detection is now more lenient, and should follow the same rules as PostgreSQL.

body:
Thanks for the PR! Great to get this working - left some comments. Also had the clanker do a review:

## Review: code quality and maintainability

### Overall

The core design is sound:
- It builds an owned `QueryNode`/`ParsedExpression` tree rather than concatenating strings.
- It is split into one file per operator family.
- It fails closed: unknown operators and types become "unsupported" rather than producing wrong SQL.
- The tests use a strict round-trip against the existing expected results as the oracle. Almost none compare exact SQL text.

The problem is how far it spreads into core. The central query path, the sqllogictest runner, table functions, serialization and eight existing test configs all now carry exporter concerns. On top of that, the exporter encodes knowledge of specific function names and optimizer rewrites. Ordinary changes to functions, types or optimizer rules will then break export, or fail CI under the new verify config, far from where the change was made.

### Major issues

#### Integration into core

1. **Every sqllogictest command pays for the verifier, even when it is off** (`test/sqlite/sqllogic_command.cpp:387-441`).
   - Each command builds a `SQLExportCollectionScope`, registers a `ClientContextState`, takes records and fabricates `"ORIGINAL_BEFORE_QUERY"` records.
   - The existing body was re-indented into a lambda.
   - This should be skipped entirely unless configured.

2. **The verifier is threaded through ClientContext's prepare path** (`client_context.cpp:543-610`).
   - This adds a new `CreatePreparedStatementWithRetry` layer and an `optional_ptr<SQLExportVerification>` parameter on `CreatePreparedStatementInternal`.
   - The rebind catch now checks `HasVerifierException()`.
   - A new `ActiveQueryContext::error_query` changes the error-reporting path for every query.
   - A single gated hook after optimize would contain all of this.

3. **`ExplainSQLVerificationOverride` bypasses `SET`** (`sqllogic_command.cpp:259-292`). It pokes `LocalUserSettings` directly and calls `DebugVerifySqlExportSetting::OnSet` by hand. This is fragile coupling to settings internals.

4. **A new serialized field exists only for the exporter.** `ExtraOperatorInfo::has_pushed_projection` (`nodes.json` property 105) is a permanent format addition whose only purpose is to let the exporter refuse. `ExtraOperatorInfo` is profiling/display metadata, so it is the wrong home anyway.

5. **Too many sources of truth for which tests run where.**
   - Skip lists were added to 8 existing configs: `disable_optimizer`, `encryption`, `v1_storage`, `v1_storage_block_size_16kB`, `force_storage_restart`, `verification_projection`, `verify_aggregate_state_export`.
   - An 82-entry hand-curated `strict_manifest.txt` has no-op `!` exclusions and a comment sitting above the wrong entry.
   - `select-strict` in the corpus script would overwrite that manifest and lose the curated comments.
   - Exclusions are duplicated between `report_manifest.txt` and `verify_sql_export_supported.json`.

6. **CI cost is roughly triple coverage.** `verify_sql_export_supported.json` becomes a full extra unittest pass (`Makefile:537`). The workflow also runs `make test_sql_export` (the strict manifest, one process per file) plus a Python selftest, and uploads artifacts on every run.

7. **`scripts/sql_export_corpus.py` (582 lines) is hard to justify.**
   - It contains a 200-line `run()`.
   - Its provenance block hashes every untracked file in the repo and embeds `CMakeCache.txt`.
   - `selftest()` is a home-grown test DSL with sqllogictests embedded as Python strings.
   - It relies on POSIX-only calls.
   - `scripts/test_sql_export_corpus.py` is never invoked by any target.

#### Exporter design

8. **Any registered custom cast disables export of default casts** (`bound_expression_sql_exporter.cpp:373-387`). The guard is `CastFunctionSet::HasRegisteredCastFunctions()`, so loading ICU or JSON (both register casts) makes every default-only bound cast unexportable. It also reaches the context through `get_mutable()` on a const-held pointer, which is effectively a `const_cast`.

9. **Function names and optimizer rewrites are hard-coded in the exporter.**
   - `sql_export_functions.cpp` special-cases `date_part`/`datepart`, `row`, `struct_pack`, `struct_update`, `write_log`, and the collated `min`/`max` → `arg_min`/`arg_max` rewrite.
   - `sql_export_window.cpp:72-147` reverse-engineers RANGE offsets by pattern-matching `+`/`-` calls by name.
   - The unbind callback on functions already exists and is used elsewhere; this knowledge belongs there.

10. **`ColumnBindingResolver` special-cases `EXPLAIN_SQL`** (`column_binding_resolver.cpp:20-27`). This is needed only because the export happens during physical planning. Producing the string right after optimization, the way the logical-plan EXPLAIN output is produced, would remove the hack.

11. **The `TableFunction::to_sql` API has a large contract that nothing checks** (`table_function.hpp:430-452`).
    - The header lists the required column order, ordinality handling and file filters bound to a magic table index.
    - It then says: "The exporter does not verify the returned query… can produce invalid or incorrect SQL."
    - Adoption is ad hoc: `duckdb_tables()` works but `duckdb_columns()`, `duckdb_views()` and about 45 others don't. The three hand-registrations shown use three different spellings.
    - Better: a declarative "reconstructible from arguments" default, and have the exporter do the projection and filter wrapping itself.

12. **A second renderer for constants** (`sql_export_constants.cpp`). It runs parallel to `Value::ToSQLString` and has its own INTERVAL, GEOMETRY, MAP and LIST constructor choices. Every new type or literal quirk now has to be fixed in two places.

13. **Programmer errors are reported as user-facing "unsupported" errors.**
    - There are about 30 `InternalInvariant` sites plus the pivot, secure-view and plan-verifier null checks. These should be `D_ASSERT`.
    - They roughly double the size of each handler and duplicate the `LogicalPlanVerifier` that already runs first.

#### Tests

14. **Test flakiness and lost coverage.**
    - 11 tests use `max_execution_time` as a pass/fail condition. That will be flaky under debug, sanitizer and verify configs, and a skip reason in the PR itself admits native execution exceeds the deadline.
    - The deleted `bound_expression_sql_export.cpp` (2,875 lines) had negative internal tests with no replacement: the deserializer restoring context after exceptions, bound-operator admission, and class/type combination validation. The PR should either justify dropping them or restore them.

### Minor issues

- **Boilerplate:**
  - `if (x.HasError()) return ...Failure(x.GetIssues());` appears about 90 times.
  - There are four identical single-issue `Failure` wrappers.
  - The WHERE-conjunction builder is repeated in 5 places.
  - `QualifiedName("system","main",...)` is spelled out inline 19–22 times, even though a helper exists.
  - The `LogicalPlanSQLExportChild` struct just wraps a single `unique_ptr`.
- **Stringly-typed codes:**
  - 37 feature/issue strings with no enum, which C++ tests match on.
  - The verifier record has 4 enums, 6 bools and free-form `code`/`phase` strings.
  - Three separate switches map issue codes to "unsupported".
- **Leakage and style:**
  - `table_scan.cpp` gains 114 lines of AST-building code with parser includes.
  - `aggregate_export.cpp` now depends on the planner exporter.
  - `FILE_FILTER_TABLE_INDEX` is referenced from `hive_partitioning.cpp`.
  - The `_internal.hpp` headers sit in the public include tree without banners.
  - The two result types (`TableFunctionToSQLResult` vs `LogicalPlanSQLExportExtensionResult`) use different conventions.
- **Oversized functions:** `ExportWindowFunction` (~210 lines), `ExportPivot` (~160), `ExportScalarFunction` (~165 lines with a dozen chained bools), and the convoluted side channel in `ExportLimitExpression`.
- **Weak or brittle test regexes:**
  - Vacuous patterns such as `.*=.*`, `.*<.*` and `.*NOT.*` in `structural_expressions.test`.
  - The opposite problem: regexes pinned to generated aliases (`r[0-9]+(c0, c1)`) and `system.main.` qualification, even though the PR says formatting isn't stable.
- **Unrelated changes to split out:**
  - the `unittest.cpp` stack-probe rewrite
  - the sqllogictest temp-dir layout change
  - PIVOT, macro and view error-text rewording
  - the shell trailing-newline fix
  - the `is_repeatable` semantics change (UNKNOWN → NON_REPEATABLE)
  - removal of the `break` in the skipif loop

### Suggested changes before merge

1. Reduce the verifier to a single post-optimize hook that costs nothing when off. Leave the sqllogictest runner untouched unless the verifier is configured, and move the ~400 lines of reporting model and JSON out of `src/main` and the runner.
2. Replace the manifests, config skip lists and Python selftests with a globbed directory and in-test `require` checks. Drop the corpus script, or cut it down to a small tool that isn't run in CI.
3. Put function-specific export logic on the functions through the unbind hook. Reuse or fix `Value::ToSQLString`. Narrow the custom-cast guard.
4. Simplify `to_sql` to "return the source invocation", with the exporter doing the wrapping, and make reconstruction from constant arguments the default.
5. Switch internal invariants to `D_ASSERT`. Add propagation, conjunction and system-function helpers.
6. Split out the unrelated changes. Given the size, the feature itself would also review better as a sequence of PRs: retention prerequisites, the exporter, EXPLAIN (SQL), then the verifier.

My `AnalyzeWKB` restructure (from `IsAtEnd()` to `geometries_remaining`) started the counter at 1, so it always reads at least one byte — a 0-byte blob throws where the old loop ran zero iterations. body:
Thanks! I took a closer look at the crash.

It turns out to be a use-after-free: when the filter prunes the input to empty, `PropagateStatistics(LogicalLimit&)` replaces the root `LogicalLimit`, destroying it. But `StatisticsPropagator` still holds an `optional_ptr` to that freed root, which `CompressedMaterialization` immediately dereferences via `root->ResolveOperatorTypes()`.

This PR holds a `unique_ptr<LogicalOperator>&` reference to the root instead, so root replacements don't leave a dangling pointer. #25932 touches `CompressedMaterialization` binding remapping, which seems to be at a different layer (after the crash point), so it might not fully prevent the UAF.

Could someone please approve the CI run for this PR? Thanks!

body:
#### **Proposal: Offset-Based Stratified Sniffing to Address Out-of-Sample Rounding**

I've been trying to solve the silent rounding of out-of-sample data (e.g, a 1.5 -> 2 appearing after a BIGINT sample).

My initial approach was to force strict = true in TrySimpleIntegerCast to atleast throw a Conversion Error instead of silently rounding the value. However, this exposed a structural conflict: the parallel I/O scanner occasionally leaks \r bytes across buffer boundaries, and somehow strict = false was silently accepting these leaks. Enforcing strict casting breaks tests like test_rrrn_parallel.test.

I believe the root cause is the sniffer's linear 20,480-row blindspot. This isn't a viable solution for scanning uncertain datatypes in a csv file. 

I'd like to propose Offset-Based Stratified Sniffing:

1) Reuse the parallel scanner's boundary-seeking logic.
2) Sample the file at 0%, 33%, 66%, and 90% byte offsets.
3) This catches late-arriving schema anomalies during Phase 1 without increasing the CPU parsing budget.

I will also try to make it more efficient and accurate during the process of development. This will fix the silent rounding of late-arriving DOUBLE or anyother values into BIGINT columns. 

**I have some question for the duckdb team:**
Q1 Is my current solution aligning with current CSV sniffer architecture?
Q2 Is there a preferred approach for stratified sampling (for example: sequential scan vs. parallel seek)?

I would be happy to draft an implementation and submit a PR.
pr_title: Fix out-of-sample type divergence in CSV scanner by imposing strict integer casting

body:
Hi @jaiswalvikas9991, @lnkuiper — I went back to this PR after receiving @lnkuiper's comment on #25133:

> Could we extend the rewrite approach instead? It should cover ENUM as well as VARCHAR, and handle the safe false-or-NULL predicate-root case in DML without a plan-wide HasSideEffects() check.

Re-examining this PR against that question surfaced one correctness issue and one way to narrow the DML side, both with fixes and tests on this PR: https://github.com/jaiswalvikas9991/duckdb/pull/1

**1. Correctness: folding ignores uncommitted appends of the same transaction**

`ConstantOrNullSimplification` folds `constant_or_null(c, x)` into the constant `c` when `NotNullExpressionAnalyzer` proves `x` non-NULL. That proof comes from `table->GetStatistics()`, which only covers **committed** row groups. Rows appended by an *earlier statement of the same transaction* live in `LocalStorage`: the scan sees them, the statistics do not — and since the query itself contains no DML, the `!plan->HasSideEffects()` gate does not catch it. The fold then drops the filter and the freshly appended NULL rows slip through:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(i INTEGER);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (NULL);
-- i * 2 <> 5 rewrites to constant_or_null(TRUE, i) via move_constants
SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE i * 2 <> 5;  -- returns 4, expected 3
```

The same applies to the full-domain ENUM `IN` producer added here (`m IN (full domain)` → `constant_or_null(TRUE, m)`). The fix is on the analyzer side: before trusting statistics in the `LOGICAL_GET` branch, check whether the current transaction holds uncommitted appends for that table, and refuse the NOT-NULL proof if so. That closes the hole for all three consumers at once (`ConstantOrNullSimplification`, `Deliminator`, `PushdownMarkJoin`), not just the fold in this PR.

**2. DML: the safe false-or-NULL root does not need a plan-wide gate — but the fold does**

Rather than removing the plan-wide `HasSideEffects()` check (which would reintroduce issue 1 for e.g. DML CTEs), I split the pass into two capabilities:

- *Shape-only rewrites* — `NOT(constant_or_null(true, x)) → constant_or_null(false, x)` and NOT-over-constant folding — keep every input evaluated per row and never consult statistics, so they are safe on all plans, DML included. On top of that, `FilterStatisticsOptimizer` already prunes `constant_or_null(false, x)` as `FILTER_FALSE_OR_NULL` *unconditionally* (no row can pass), so full-domain `NOT IN` collapses to an empty result inside `DELETE`/`UPDATE` plans without any stats dependency.
- *Folding to a constant* drops the per-row evaluation of the inputs, so it stays gated on the plan having no side effects.

So the direction @lnkuiper suggested is achievable for the false-or-NULL root across both producers (ENUM here, and the non-ENUM `move_constants` producer `i * 2 <> 5`), and the remaining plan-wide gate only protects the fold-to-TRUE direction, which genuinely relies on the statistics proof.

Tests covering both points (the stale-statistics scenario as a red known-issue first, then the fix, plus the DML guard behavior) live on my branch ([verify branch link]), with the analyzer fix being the key change.

body:
Thanks - had the clanker do a pass and it raised the following issues:

## Issues

1. **A NULL-free build group gets a second full hash table** (`src/execution/mark_join_refinement.cpp`, `MarkPatternRefiner::Refine`). When the probe mask and the group mask are both 0, `dropped == 0`. `Classify` still returns a non-empty `equality_mask`, so `BuildEqualityIndex` builds a hash table over the entire NULL-free build and probes it. Native probing has already evaluated exactly those pairs. A single NULL equality key anywhere in the build is enough to trigger this for every unmatched probe row. Unless nested columns are involved (nested NULLs can still produce UNKNOWN), groups with `dropped == 0` could be skipped.

2. **`NullMask` builds a `Value` for every build cell** (`MarkJoinRefinement::NullMask`). `AddChunk` calls `keys.data[col].GetValue(row).IsNull()` for every retained build row and condition column, including string copies for VARCHAR. This runs over the entire build the first time any probe chunk needs refinement. `Refine`, `ProbeEqualityIndex` and `RefineWitnessBatch` also recompute it per probe row. It should read the validity masks through the vector API instead. The same row-by-row `Value` pattern appears in `BuildRangeIndex`, `RunRangeJoin` and `RefineOneRange`.

3. **Dead code: `MarkJoinRowComparison::UpdateRangeBound`** and its `MarkRangeExtreme` helper (about 60 lines) are never called. They look like the typed fast path `RefineOneRange` was meant to use. `RefineOneRange` uses `GetValue` with `ValueOperations::GreaterThan` instead.

4. **Memory the buffer manager doesn't track, sized after memory is reserved.** `MarkJoinRefinementGroup::selections` holds a `vector<sel_t>` for every retained build row, plus `map` nodes. That is plain heap memory, not buffer-managed. The refinement and its indexes are built lazily during the probe phase, after the external-join memory reservation has been computed, so adding them to `MarkJoinSize()` doesn't feed into memory planning. `MarkJoinSize()` also walks `refinement->groups` / `indexes` without holding `mj_lock`, while other threads may be inserting indexes under that lock.

5. **Build payload is copied for residual MARK joins.** With a residual predicate, `uncorrelated_condition_rows` now keeps `condition_types + build_types` for every build row, even when the build contains no NULLs. That roughly doubles build-side memory for these joins. It would be good to measure the impact.

6. **The native probe path is slower for mixed MARK joins.** `ResolveMarkPredicates` replaces the `RowMatcher` path whenever `conditions_can_be_unknown` is set. That flag stays set once any build chunk has an allocated validity mask. On every step along a hash chain it allocates a gather `Vector` for each condition and two `SelectionVector`s, and puts two `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` bool arrays on the stack. Could you benchmark a plain `a = b AND c < d` MARK join over nullable columns against main?

7. **Timing-dependent test** (`test/sql/join/mark/hash_conjunction.test`). It runs a 16x repeated 20k x 20k MARK join under `SET max_execution_time=1000` and expects it to succeed. That will likely be flaky on sanitizer, debug or valgrind runners. It should use a much larger limit or drop the time limit.

body:
Thanks, I've addressed these in the follow-up commits:

1. Scalar groups with no dropped comparisons now skip the redundant secondary index. The 40k-row single-NULL-build case dropped from 8.15 ms to 3.02 ms.
2. NULL masks use vector validity, range preparation slices vectors, and extremum selection extracts one winning value per chunk instead of boxing every row.
3. Removed both unused helpers.
4. Row selections and cache metadata now use buffer-managed allocation. Lazy cache construction updates the hash join's reservation, external partition budgets account for persistent caches, and size inspection is locked. I also checked construction failures with retained prepared plans: speculative reservations are reconciled before re-throwing, and subsequent execution recovers.
5. The payload copy remains. With 40k rows and roughly 256-byte strings, peak buffer memory is 57.9 MB versus 42.2 MB on current upstream. A later NULL-key probe can still need that payload even when the build has no NULL keys.
6. Comparison scratch is now allocated lazily and reused, and an allocated validity bitmap alone no longer enables UNKNOWN handling. The nullable equality-plus-range benchmark measured 1.422 ms here, 1.417 ms before these changes, and 1.262 ms on current upstream. That remaining overhead is still present. These changes did not measurably improve this particular workload.
7. Removed the one-second deadline, retaining the result and HASH_JOIN assertions.

body:
Thanks - I had another look and I think structurally this is the wrong fix here. Mark joins exist purely to facilitate correlated subqueries and correlated subqueries cannot produce these plans. I think it would be better to throw an error in these kinds of joins instead. 

The current PR seems to be addressing the fact that mark joins can only be "sort of" round tripped through SQL right now. This means that a logical-plan-to-sql needs to take a different path than the original plan. That seems like not a great idea, because now the original plan is different from logical-plan-to-sql. Instead I think a better path forward is to make these types of mark joins unsupported and fix up the SQL round-trip to enable full round-tripping of mark joins.

Below is some AI thoughts:

```
  Why the explicit SQL form goes wrong. SQL has no syntax for mark_types, so it is empty. The same conditions (g IS NOT DISTINCT FROM g', a = x) then run
  through the generic MARK path, which tracks NULLs for the whole build side instead of per group. That's why g=1 comes back as NULL instead of false in the
  earlier test.

  Rebuilding the metadata from the conditions is exact, not a heuristic. IS NOT DISTINCT FROM never returns NULL. So for a conjunction of the form k1 IS NOT
  DISTINCT FROM k1' AND … AND a op x:
  - pairs from a different group are definitely false;
  - pairs in the same group evaluate to a op x.

  Folding over all pairs gives exactly the per-group semantics the grouped path computes. This holds whether the join came from a subquery or was written by
  hand.

  What that means for the PR. The decorrelated-as-SQL fix is TryGetMarkJoinGroupTypes (~70 lines, planner only) plus two lines in plan_comparison_join.cpp, and
  after that it runs on the existing execution code. The ~2,800 lines of new execution machinery serve only shapes no decorrelated plan produces: a = x AND c >
  d, residual/arbitrary predicates, and non-grouping NULL-safe mixes. These include the retained build rows, NULL-pattern refinement, the IE-join enumeration
  and the buffer-managed indexes.

  What I'd do instead:
  1. In plan_joinref.cpp, when an explicit MARK join has the shape IS NOT DISTINCT FROM…, <single comparison>, fill mark_types there. It's better at bind time
     than in the physical planner, so the optimizers see the same logical plan a subquery would produce.
  2. Keep the other safe shapes (a single comparison, or only plain = conditions).
  3. Throw NotImplementedException for everything else, which also removes the existing crash on arbitrary conditions.

  That covers every shape a real decorrelated plan can produce and adds nothing to execution. The condition order needs checking: the grouped path assumes the
  grouping keys come first and the comparison last. TryGetMarkJoinGroupTypes already requires that order, so any other order would fall into the "unsupported"
  branch rather than give wrong results.
```

Thanks for working on this! The collation issue definitely needs fixing, and preserving an original representative for aggregates such as `list` is an important part of that.

I'd prefer to address this in the multi-stage aggregate rewrite, though. We're moving towards expressing DISTINCT aggregates as ordinary aggregations over a deduplicated input, with CTEs sharing that input where needed. Eventually, I'd like to remove the dedicated DISTINCT machinery from the physical aggregate operators.

This PR takes us in the opposite direction: it adds normalization and representative-value handling to the physical DISTINCT path, then excludes collated aggregates from the rewrite. That makes the old path necessary for correctness and leaves us with functionality we'll need to move again before we can remove it.

Could we instead extend `CreateDistinctBranch` to group by the normalized comparison keys and retain original values through `first(...)` aggregates? The final non-distinct aggregate would then consume those representatives. We already use this approach when binding collated `GROUP BY` expressions, so that should provide a useful reference, and perhaps an opportunity to share some of the construction logic.

There is still a transition to account for: DISTINCT rewriting can currently be disabled, so supporting collation in the rewrite won't immediately let us delete the physical implementation. But I'd like the rewrite to be the primary implementation of these semantics. We can then work towards making that lowering mandatory.

The result tests here would be useful for that implementation too. I'd also add plan checks showing that collated DISTINCT aggregates continue through the multi-stage rewrite, including when mixed with other aggregates.

body:
I've removed some unreachable parquet time functions.

Reaching LogicalTypeId::TIME_NS means:

Parquet annotation | Physical type | DuckDB type -- | -- | -- TIME(MILLIS) | INT32 | TIME TIME(MICROS) | INT64 | TIME TIME(NANOS) | INT64 | TIME_NS

The Parquet schema explicitly requires INT32 for milliseconds and INT64 for microseconds/nanoseconds in third_party/parquet/parquet.thrift:383.

DuckDB’s shared schema mapping likewise maps only UNIT_NS to TIME_NS; milliseconds and microseconds map to TIME in extension/parquet/include/parquet_column_schema.hpp:73.

Therefore, inside the TIME_NS case:

  • A 4-byte statistic cannot be valid: that encoding belongs to TIME(MILLIS), which derives as TIME.
  • UNIT_MS cannot occur because it derives as TIME.
  • UNIT_MICROS cannot occur because it also derives as TIME.
  • The only valid combination is TIME_NS + UNIT_NS + INT64.

The new code consequently does the exact required operation:

Load<int64_t>(stats_data)

and interprets that value directly as nanoseconds through ParquetIntToTimeNs extension/parquet/parquet_timestamp.cpp:88.

The two checks distinguish failure classes:

  • Wrong byte width means malformed external Parquet statistics, hence InvalidInputException.
  • TIME_NS with non-nanosecond type info violates DuckDB’s internal derived-schema invariant, hence InternalException.

The old INT32, UNIT_MS, and UNIT_MICROS paths were generic conversion support for combinations that schema derivation cannot produce. A malformed TIME(NANOS) column physically encoded as INT32 is now rejected instead of being silently accepted.

body:
A couple of questions about the abstraction here.

First, should `EXPLAIN` as a table reference be allowed to correlate with the outer query? E.g.:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM t,
LATERAL (
    EXPLAIN
    SELECT * FROM u WHERE u.i = t.i
);
```

If this is valid, the semantics get a bit murky: are we explaining one parameterized plan, or effectively evaluating `EXPLAIN` per outer row? My instinct is that correlation should probably be unsupported, but it would be good to make that an explicit design choice rather than an implementation limitation.

The other question is whether this really wants to be a normal `TableRef` / logical operator internally.

I don't think a scalar function fits particularly well, and something like:

```sql
FROM explain('SELECT ...')
```

would be awkward because it turns the query into a string and introduces another parsing/binding boundary.

That said, a table-function-like implementation has one nice property: it gives `EXPLAIN` a very clear optimization boundary. The child query is what we're trying to inspect, so outer rewrites shouldn't leak into it. The special handling for `LOGICAL_EXPLAIN` in things like column pruning / join ordering feels like a consequence of representing it as part of the normal surrounding logical plan.

So I like the syntax here, and keeping the inner query as a real `QueryNode` seems preferable. I'm mostly wondering whether `EXPLAIN` should be treated internally as a stronger opaque boundary, possibly with table-function-like execution semantics, rather than as a normal logical operator that optimizer passes need to explicitly avoid crossing.

And separately, I'd lean toward keeping correlation unsupported unless there's a clear use case and execution model for it.

I feel like I agree with @carlopi that we don't necessarily need to get rid of `ParserOptions`. There's now also three PRs in-flight that attempt to fix the same issue it seems: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/25973 https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/26020 and this one.

I think, now with the `DialectExtension` and `GrammarExtension` we need to be more explicit whether a query is parsed with a context-aware parser or built-in. However, I don't think every parser needs the full `ClientContext`. There are internal cases where we parse built-in DuckSQL without any `ClientContext`. I think `ParserOptions` provides a boundary for grammar specific options without bringing along the entire `ClientContext`.

So what I think would be good is that we make it more explicit whether you create a context-aware parser with the possibility of `GrammarExtensions`, custom `ParserOptions` etc. or a shared built-in parser with only parses the default DuckSQL but isn't recreated upon every call (which is part of the problem we are currently seeing): 
```cpp
Parser parser(context);  // Connection-specific settings and extensions
Parser parser(options);  // Custom parser configuration
auto parser = Parser::GetBuiltinParser();  // built-in DuckDB grammar and settings
```
The `GetBuiltInParser` can always reuse a shared compiled-grammar as that will never change, so the construction overhead is gone.

body:
There might be an issue here with indexes from extensions that aren't loaded. `WriteTable` now binds every unbound index during automatic checkpoints, and `IndexBinder::BindIndex` throws a `MissingExtensionException` when the index type isn't registered. So a database with e.g. an RTREE/HNSW index, opened without that extension, would fail its next automatic checkpoint, even if that checkpoint was triggered by a write to an unrelated table.

Maybe we can only bind indexes that actually have buffered replays? That would narrow the failure down to "extension not loaded + WAL replay buffered changes for that extension's index", instead of failing whenever an extension index isn't loaded. `TableIndexList::Bind` currently binds every unbound index on the table, so a table-level `HasBufferedReplays()` check wouldn't be enough; it would need to filter per index. Would be good to add a test for this too.

Also, not sure, but I'm wondering if we'd want to skip the automatic checkpoint upfront (and keep the WAL, similar to the no-context path in `CreateCheckpoint`) if it turns out we can't bind an index. I think if this happens mid-checkpoint, the exception is caught in `SingleFileStorageManager::CreateCheckpoint` and we end up invalidating the database.

With four threads, TPC-DS SF10 Q95 increases from **165.5 ms to 209.1 ms (+26.4%)**, and Q21 from **13.1 ms to 14.6 ms (+11.6%)**. These results persist through 30 and 100 confirmation samples per build, respectively.

The job is green because individual query regressions produce warnings. Failure is based on the suite's geometric mean.

Please investigate Q95 first by comparing the plans, published runtime filters, and build/probe profiles against the CI baseline. pr_title: fix: external hash join dropping rows through a partial bloom filter

body:
Accumulating the bloom filter during `Sink` looks like a reasonable way to address the root cause. A filter pushed into the probe scan must cover every build partition, including partitions processed in later external join rounds. Collecting hashes as the build rows arrive establishes that completeness independently of which partitions are currently materialized. Sealing before publication and retaining shared ownership in the scan expressions also make the intended lifecycle clearer.

Before merging, I would like to see the following addressed:

1. **Make the initial allocation respect the memory budget.** The overestimated-build case in my inline comment produces only two build rows, but this change allocates a 32 MiB filter from the estimate and fails under a 25 MB limit. The parent succeeds. Please bound the speculative allocation or omit the optional filter when it cannot fit. Folding in `Seal()` happens too late to prevent this failure. Add an overestimated-build regression alongside the existing underestimated-build test.

2. **Check the cost of the shared construction path.** Every local hash table now inserts into the same filter through atomic updates. That may be a reasonable trade-off, but I have not measured it. Please compare the parent and this change with one and multiple threads, using both mostly distinct and duplicate-heavy build keys. Include an in-memory case where a prefix-range filter or perfect hash join is ultimately selected: those cases now pay for bloom-filter construction without publishing it. The measurements should help establish whether the initial eligibility check needs to be more selective.

3. **Keep the completeness fix distinguishable from the sizing policy.** Density-based folding is not what makes the external join correct. Collecting the complete key set is. I would consider separating folding into a follow-up unless it is necessary for an acceptable memory footprint here. If it stays, please add focused coverage showing that folding preserves membership and that a saturated filter is safely omitted.

The original spill reproducer returns the correct result with this change, and the focused tests and additional differential checks passed. The approach could work to ensure completeness, but I would request changes for the allocation regression and want evidence on the shared construction cost before endorsing it as the general path for eligible hash joins.

body:
Thanks @Mytherin — based on @kliszaq's testing of the PR head against real SQL Server 2025 CETAS files, the `blob` mode is needed rather than niche.

`int96_as = 'timestamp_ns'` does preserve the nanosecond part, but INT96 files written by SQL Server/Spark commonly use `0001-01-01` and `9999-12-31` (e.g. `datetime2(7)` = `9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999`) as open-ended sentinel dates. Those are valid INT96 values but fall outside the `TIMESTAMP_NS` range (1677–2262), so `timestamp_ns` hard-fails the whole read, whereas the default only truncates the sub-microsecond digits. `blob` is the only mode that reads the full 0001–9999 range losslessly.

I added regression coverage for this to `int96_as.test`: an INT96 file containing `0001-01-01` and `9999-12-31` where the default reads it (at microseconds), `timestamp_ns` raises a conversion error, and `blob` round-trips the raw 12 bytes. Also added a test for dictionary-encoded INT96 read as `blob` (previously only `timestamp_ns` was covered there).

If exposing a raw BLOB is undesirable, a `STRUCT(julian_day INTEGER, nanos_of_day BIGINT)` would be equivalent — but some full-range output is required to solve #25857 for these files.

body:
Thanks both — my vote is for the struct, decomposed as `DATE` + `TIME_NS` as @Mytherin suggested.
 
The `±infinity` saturation avoids the hard failure, but it is silently lossy, which for our use case is worse than an error: `9999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999`, `9999-12-31 00:00:00` and any year-3000 value all become `+infinity`, and `0001-01-01` and a year-1500 value both become `-infinity`. These are valid `datetime2` values that SQL Server/Spark write to INT96, and a reader that needs to round-trip them (the motivation for #25857) cannot recover the original from `infinity`. It also only works while the out-of-range values happen to be sentinels — historical dates before 1677 are ordinary data.
 
`STRUCT(date DATE, time TIME_NS)` is lossless over the whole range INT96 can express in practice, stays fully typed (no client-side byte decoding, unlike `blob`), and is easy to consume: `s.date`, `s.time`, `epoch_ns(s.time)`, or recombine into `TIMESTAMP_NS` when the caller knows the data fits. So I'd be happy with `blob` being dropped in favour of the struct.
 
If only one mode can be kept, I'd pick the struct: a caller who wants `TIMESTAMP_NS` can derive it from the struct, but not the other way round.

body:
Thanks for the PR - code looks good but I'm mostly worried about the perf aspect of these changes. Some AI suggestions:

> 1. Validation is per value where it could be per array. ValidateAndGetDictionaryOffset runs the INT32_MIN check, the sign branch, and the > dictionary_size bounds check on every string, and CreateDictionaryEntry adds a monotonicity check plus two more on the negative path. Since the offsets are monotonic by construction, a single pass over the int32_t offsets array per segment (or per vector) validating bounds + ordering would let the inner loop go back to the old branchless abs(cur) - abs(prev) form. The offsets are already being read, and that pass vectorizes.
> 2. Select/StringFetchRow re-validate the previous offset for every row. GetDictionaryEntry calls ValidateAndGetDictionaryOffset(offsets[i-1]) in addition to the current one, doubling the check cost — which is why the Select path (+116%) is worse than the sequential one. I verified this by building a variant that does the same thing in the sequential loop: it went to +288%, worse than the PR. (Corollary: the loop-carried previous_dictionary_offset accumulator is not the problem — removing it costs more than it saves.)
> 3. UncompressedStringSegmentState::GetHandle gained an O(n) std::find over on_disk_blocks plus a TotalBlocks() call that takes the block-manager mutex, on first touch of each overflow block, under block_lock. It's amortized by the handles map, so it didn't show in my overflow benchmark (2000 strings), but it's O(n²) in overflow blocks per segment over a cold scan. Cheap to fix with a set.

Could you have a look and do some perf analysis + try to minimize perf impact?

body:
Just to clarify: for raw vector writes and CDC appends, the contract is that VARCHAR data must already contain valid UTF-8. Those operations don’t validate it themselves. The V2 CAPI exposes a UTF-8 validation function so callers and higher-level APIs can build checked construction helpers before writing the resulting values.

The stable C++ API changes here provide these helpers/show how this is done: Arena::AddString validates during construction, while Arena::AddStringUnsafe skips validation when the caller already knows the text is valid. Vector::SetString then places the resulting value without validating it again. AssignString and AssignStringUnsafe are convenience methods combining construction and placement.

This is nice IMO because we have an explicit place to validate text without repeating the check whenever a value is written or reused. The requirement for valid UTF-8 stays the same whichever path you use. Separately we could validate internally for functions that receive texts outside of hot paths and just always do the validation there. 

I think the main thing is also just making this as explicit as possible.

Thanks for checking! You're right that the reporter's exact SQL no longer crashes on the dev branch — but the underlying hazard is still present there: `RemoveColumnsFromLogicalGet` still interleaves `filter_expressions.push_back()` with `VisitExpression(&filter_expressions.back())` in the same loop, so a vector reallocation can still invalidate the `BoundColumnRefExpression` references registered by earlier `VisitExpression` calls (`src/optimizer/remove_unused_columns.cpp`, ~line 1127).

The query plan likely changed on this branch so that specific query no longer reaches the pattern — the fix is a defensive port of the v2.0-cyanoptera change (#25634) that makes the collection order safe regardless of which filters arrive. Happy to close if you'd rather not carry the hardening on this branch.

body:
> where we push COUNT(*), MIN, MAX, etc and evaluate them using row group stats

This unfortunately isn't a generalisable approach. Vortex doesn't have row groups in the Parquet sense, and zone map granularity (8192 rows) is much smaller, so scheduling costs if we set partition = zone map overweight the benefits greatly. One example of this is you need to report partition index while pushing data to DataChunk. In result you'd return from scan function every 8k rows which gives very bad performance.

Reason number two is this doesn't work if aggregates are filtered. This also makes sense because you generally don't know what to do if a partition is partially filtered out. In Vortex we can read and accumulate the post-filter chunk ourselves.

Reason number three is that our stats may be imprecise (in which case we need to load the chunk and evaluate it).

I suggest adding the new callback for readers which don't look like Parquet or have different granularity (like Vortex) and keep the current implementation for formats where partition stats are enough.

Thanks for the comments - but I'm still not really seeing a good reason to introduce the extra callbacks here. At least in the current suggested implementation it seems that the main motivation behind this callback is to use metadata to answer aggregates, which is already enabled by the partition stats callback optimizer. Perhaps that callback can instead be modified / extended to make it work for Vortex?

> Reason number two is this doesn't work if aggregates are filtered. This also makes sense because you generally don't know what to do if a partition is partially filtered out. In Vortex we can read and accumulate the post-filter chunk ourselves.

> Reason number three is that our stats may be imprecise (in which case we need to load the chunk and evaluate it).

For `COUNT(*)`, it should be possible to emit chunks that only have a count for the filtered scenario as a `EMPTY` column would be the only column required in the projection list. This should have a very minimal overhead, i.e. it shouldn't be necessary to emit any actual values.

body:
> main motivation behind this callback is to use metadata to answer 
aggregates

Yes, and also support this in queries with filters.
Current distinction is that aggregates propagation happens in optimizer phase (row group is large, reading it and getting partition stats is cheap), but our implementation executes in run phase, because we determine whether the row group is to be skipped/populated from metadata only during query execution (since a row group ~ zone map is 8192 rows, reading it separately from file contents is expensive).

I can in theory tweak the callback optimizer to run during scan and support filtering to avoid scanning partitions which can be supplied from metadata (although this would be a much bigger change), but I can't change granularity of row group partitioning in Vortex.

Returning from Scan() every 8192 rows is impractical from performance perspective.

body:
The current implementation has an outstanding issue where a checkpoint invalidates all `Index&` references. This happens for example in the spatial extension, which stores the `Index&` in the bind data and later uses it during scan execution.

Storing `Index&` references was safe previously, as the `Index` itself was stable across its lifetime. This PR changes this model: During checkpointing a swap makes `entry->index` (from the `TableIndexList`) point to the shadow index. Thus making any existing references to the old `Index` stale.

body:
More substantial question concerning performance, this is where I would be curious to maybe run some benchmarks and make sure we don't run into any serious slowdowns: 

Previously we had this as a scenario:

1) ART is checkpointed already 
2) queries touch the ART, load some saved buffers into working memory. Buffers remain clean (just doing reads)
3) A later checkpoint processes the index, allocations stay in memory
4) Queries read from the allocations that didn't get evicted 

Now we’re creating replacements and discarding those working allocations when we install the shadow. Of course, this doesn't mean we have to fetch from disk necessarily, since they might stay in memory still, but this is where I'd be curious to see if we run into any regressions + if so, if we can do something here to have the old optimization. Or, if there are regressions but they aren't too bad, we just accept the trade-off and can come back to this as a follow up.
