Thanks for the PR! Sounds good to me, the clanker just found this hang:

```sql
# name: test/sql/storage/checkpoint/checkpoint_after_prepared_dml.test
# description: A cached prepared DELETE/UPDATE must not hold the table's checkpoint lock after it finishes
# group: [checkpoint]

load __TEST_DIR__/checkpoint_after_prepared_dml.db

statement ok
CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT i FROM range(100000) t(i);

statement ok
CREATE TABLE lists AS SELECT i, [i] AS l FROM range(10000) t(i);

statement ok
CREATE TABLE pk(i INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, j INTEGER);

statement ok
INSERT INTO pk SELECT i, i FROM range(10000) t(i);

statement ok
CHECKPOINT

# prepared statements without parameters keep their physical plan between executions
statement ok
PREPARE del AS DELETE FROM t WHERE i < 10;

statement ok
EXECUTE del

statement ok
CHECKPOINT

# re-executing the same cached plan
statement ok
EXECUTE del

statement ok
CHECKPOINT

query I
SELECT count(*) FROM t
----
99990

# DELETE with RETURNING
statement ok
PREPARE del_ret AS DELETE FROM t WHERE i = 10 RETURNING i;

query I
EXECUTE del_ret
----
10

statement ok
CHECKPOINT

# UPDATE on a LIST column is executed as a delete + insert
statement ok
PREPARE upd_list AS UPDATE lists SET l = [42] WHERE i = 5;

statement ok
EXECUTE upd_list

statement ok
CHECKPOINT

# UPDATE on an indexed column is executed as a delete + insert
statement ok
PREPARE upd_pk AS UPDATE pk SET i = i + 100000 WHERE i < 10;

statement ok
EXECUTE upd_pk

statement ok
CHECKPOINT

# the automatic checkpoint at commit of the prepared statement itself
statement ok
SET checkpoint_threshold='1KB'

statement ok
PREPARE del_auto AS DELETE FROM t WHERE i < 50000;

statement ok
EXECUTE del_auto

statement ok
RESET checkpoint_threshold

restart

query I
SELECT count(*) FROM t
----
50000

query I
SELECT l FROM lists WHERE i = 5
----
[42]

query II
SELECT count(*), min(i) FROM pk WHERE i >= 100000
----
10	100000

```

Caused by the `PhysicalOperator` (which contains the global state) being cached in the prepared statement. Suggested fix is to release the lock in `PhysicalDelete::Finalize` to prevent it from being held after the operator is finished.

A better / more structural fix would be to release the global state after we're done with an operator but that's more of a v2.0 and onwards fix.
pr_title: Acquire the table's checkpoint lock once per statement

body:
Thanks!

> Suggested fix is to release the lock in PhysicalDelete::Finalize to prevent it from being held after the operator is finished.

That would work well for the happy case, but does not cover failures / query interruptions (as then Finalize isn't called).

I've slightly reworked the PR here to better deal with that too, getting closer back to the original design: The global sink state of PhysicalDelete now acquires the lock first, once, on the single thread that initializes the pipeline. As soon as the first pipeline task actually runs, it clears it and instead uses the tasks' local states as before.

> A better / more structural fix would be to release the global state after we're done with an operator but that's more of a v2.0 and onwards fix.

Agreed.

Note that for 2.x I plan to make this table-level checkpoint lock obsolete.

body:
@Mytherin  Thanks for the guidance. Before making changes, could you clarify the intended design of `EstimateCardinality` and `RelationStatisticsHelper`? 

Currently, `EstimateCardinality` seems to be a simple estimate. The base implementation just takes the maximum cardinality of the children and caches it, so `LogicalFilter`, which does not override it, does not estimate filter selectivity. Also, the uncached path of `LogicalGet::EstimateCardinality` uses the source cardinality without estimating `table_filters`.

In contrast, `RelationStatisticsHelper::ExtractGetStats` performs a more detailed estimate using column statistics and `table_filters`, and the join-order optimizer subsequently writes that result back into the same `estimated_cardinality` field.

Therefore, an `estimated_cardinality` may come from the cheap operator-level estimate or the more detailed relation-statistics path. For this bug, `ExtractGetStats` treats `get.EstimateCardinality()` as the pre-filter source cardinality, but it may return a post-filter estimate written by an earlier relation-statistics extraction.

Should `EstimateCardinality()` remain a cheap and potentially inaccurate fallback, with the more detailed estimates kept in `RelationStatisticsHelper`? Or should `EstimateCardinality()` become the authoritative estimate and reuse the logic from `ExtractGetStats()`? 

Once I understand the intended semantics of these estimates, I can fix this issue in the appropriate layer.
pr_title: Fix duplicate table filter cardinality estimation

## CI: Thread Sanitizer failure — unrelated to this PR

Hi! The only failing check on this PR is **Thread Sanitizer**, on the httpfs extension test `secrets/create_secret_transactional.test:67`:

```
Invalid Input Error: Failed to remove non-existent secret with name "s1"
```

This looks like a pre-existing, known httpfs flake rather than a regression from this change:

- This PR only touches `src/function/cast/bignum_casts.cpp` and the two BIGNUM test files — nothing in the storage-secrets/httpfs path.
- A very similar random failure in the httpfs `secrets/*` tests is already tracked upstream in duckdb/duckdb-httpfs#375, whose root cause is an uninitialized `ExtraDropSecretInfo::persist_mode` in DuckDB's `secret_manager.cpp`/`extra_drop_info.cpp` — intermittent, state/timing dependent, which is precisely why TSAN trips on it while all other 30+ checks on this PR pass.

Happy to re-run the TSAN job, or this can be re-triggered once the upstream flake is fixed.

(AI assisted review comment); I think it's better to handle this in the aggregate/window binding, `BaseSelectBinder::BindAggregate`, rather than in the filter case. This qualified-star handling should happen before the argument-binding loop
There's a case with using the `count(t.*)` that regresses:

```
CREATE MACRO count_rows() AS count(t.*);
Binder Error:
STAR expression is not supported here

LINE 1: CREATE MACRO count_rows() AS count(t.*);
                                           ^^^
```

The same goes for window functions: 
```
 SELECT
               count(*) OVER () AS all_rows,
               count(t.*) OVER () AS qualified_rows
           FROM (VALUES (NULL::INT, NULL::INT)) AS t(x, y);
┌──────────┬────────────────┐
│ all_rows │ qualified_rows │
│  int64   │     int64      │
├──────────┼────────────────┤
│        1 │              0 │
└──────────┴────────────────┘
```
This should return 1 for both cases (PostgreSQL behavior)

I'm checking on the storage leak due to failed commits, and find this PR only covers part of the issue, working on a broader fix (WIP vhttps://github.com/dentiny/duckdb/pull/204)

| # | Failure window | How to trigger | Covered by this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Flush` fails mid-way in `AppendToIndexes`; blocks flushed but not yet merged | Commit-time unique constraint violation | No |
| 2 | Multi-table transaction: a table has not been reached by the flush loop yet, but its blocks were already flushed by `PreFlushOptimisticBlocks`; stack unwinding destroys the map without `Rollback` | Multi-table commit where one table fails | No |
| 3 | Table already merged and `PushAppend` done, then commit fails; the undo revert detaches the row groups but never frees their blocks | `debug_force_commit_failure`; the first table in a multi-table commit | Yes |

pr_title: Preserve complete predicates in nested-loop MARK, SEMI and ANTI joins

body:
I found a related nested-lateral case that appears to need additional handling beyond scalar CTE filter pushdown(v1.5.5 does not exists this problem):

```sql
CREATE TABLE person(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO person SELECT i FROM range(1000) t(i);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT max(x)
FROM (
    SELECT o.id, q.x
    FROM person o,
    LATERAL (
        SELECT r.x
        FROM person i,
        LATERAL (
            WITH RECURSIVE walk(x) USING KEY(x) AS (
                SELECT i.id
                UNION
                SELECT w.x + 1
                FROM walk w
                WHERE w.x < i.id + 2
                  AND NOT EXISTS (
                      SELECT 1
                      FROM recurring.walk visited
                      WHERE visited.x = w.x + 1
                  )
            )
            SELECT max(x) AS x FROM walk
        ) r
        WHERE i.id = o.id
        UNION ALL
        SELECT -1
    ) q
) result
WHERE id = 3;
```

The query returns 5. In our local development build, the recursive operator produces 3,000 rows: all 1,000 seeds are processed even though only id = 3 contributes to the final result.

There appear to be two obstacles:

- The domain eligibility check rejects keyed/recurring recursion, so no CTEFilterDependency is recorded for this case.
- The restriction needed by the inner producer comes from the equality join i.id = o.id, rather than a scalar filter directly above its CTE scan. Scalar predicate copying alone does not propagate that restriction.

Our local prototype preserves domain provenance from decorrelation and adds a SEMI JOIN restriction to the eligible producer, using an existing ancestor materialization while retaining the original join. For this reproducer, recursive output drops from 3,000 rows to 3, with the same result.

The prototype conservatively requires the source to be provably at most one row—here, established by the primary key and id = 3. Merely requiring a filtered source was insufficient to avoid performance regressions with non-selective predicates.

Would extending CTEFilterPusher to handle join-derived restrictions, together with an explicit safety proof for decorrelated keyed/recurring CTEs, fit the intended direction? Or would you prefer this as a separate follow-up?

The exporter already reconstructs children using the current column-binding context, so it could pass those parsed children, the bound function and its bind data to an unbind callback. The reason this is done is related to time spent in analyze vs pay-off.
Maybe less relevant now that we have fewer string compression methods to analyze, but probably still somewhat relevant.

Dict-FSST isn't really possible to estimate accurately without essentially doing a dry-run of the compression, which is expensive to do when the result might get thrown away in the end.

body:
We hit the same thing in our fork, where string columns end up much larger than ClickHouse or Parquet (ClickBench lands around 20 GB for duckdb vs ~8 GB / ~14 GB).

> Dict-FSST isn't really possible to estimate accurately without essentially doing a dry-run of the compression

IMO the separation into analyze and compress just doesn't work well for strings at all -- not only for dict_fsst. What we'd want instead is two decisions: first dict vs non-dict, and then how to compress the bytes -- uncompressed, fsst, fsst plus, zstd, lz4, zxc, etc.

The thing that makes that hard in DuckDB is that we also want to know the size after compression ahead of time, so we can produce 256 KB compressed blocks. In other formats (parquet, vortex, clickhouse, etc) you always compress some block of uncompressed data (e.g. 1MB) instead, which makes the implementation much easier and more straightforward, and there's nothing to estimate.


Strictly speaking even for integers data analyze/compress isn't good, because dictionary can be for integers too, but this way less noticable
pr_title: Fix/dict fsst size estimate

body:
@Tishj 
Three new files under `benchmark/micro/compression/dictionary/`. Two force `dict_fsst`, as the existing store benchmarks do, holding the compression constant so only the analysis cost differs. The third leaves the choice to the selection, which determines whether the estimate pays off. All three use values large enough that only a couple fit in a block — the existing `dictionary_store*` benchmarks already cover short values.

| benchmark | before | after | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| large scattered duplicates, forced `dict_fsst` | 2.194 / 2.290 | 2.386 / 2.506 | **+9%** |
| large unique values, forced `dict_fsst` | 3.260 / 3.301 | 3.307 / 3.343 | **+1%** |
| large scattered duplicates, automatic selection | 2.140 / 2.354 | 1.662 / 1.783 | **-23%** |

(min / median seconds, n=12 per side)

So the added analysis cost is roughly 1-9% of the write path, largest when duplicates exist and the hash set is actually probed. Where the estimate changes the outcome, total write time drops by 23% because the old estimate selected DICT_FSST, which then wrote ~50k near-empty segments. The added work per value is one hash plus one hash-set probe, plus an insert and a heap copy only for values new to the current block; memory stays bounded to one block's distinct values, as the set and its heap are reset at every simulated block boundary.

Method, since two things materially affected the numbers:

- `make reldebug` enables `ENABLE_SANITIZER` and `ENABLE_UBSAN` by default. Under those, everything ran about 4x slower, and the payoff looked like -52% rather than -23%, biased in favour of this change since it adds allocations and hashing. These numbers are `DISABLE_SANITIZER=1`.
- Two prebuilt binaries run alternately rather than one side then the other, 3 rounds of 4 timed iterations each, discarding the first iteration of each invocation. Without interleaving, the machine drifts between the two sides. Some "before" runs still show outliers (up to 6.1s against a 3.3s median), which is why minimums are quoted alongside medians.

body:
Hi @Mytherin, could you take a quick look at whether this PR is useful and worth maintaining upstream?

The main idea is to reuse unchanged persistent segments during checkpoint to reduce CPU and I/O for sparse updates. If this direction makes sense, I’m happy to keep improving and maintaining it.
pr_title: Reuse unchanged persistent segments during checkpoint

body:
Thanks for the PR! I think the idea is certainly interesting. One worry I have here is that this can lead to sub-optimal compression, for example if we have segments like this:

```
Block 1 - 256KB
Block 2 - 256KB
Block 3 - 256KB
Block 4 - 40KB
```

Then we update a string in block 2 and checkpoint it, but the string is slightly bigger than our previous block, we will now end up with this situation:

```
Block 1 - 256KB  (re-used)
Block 2 - 256KB  (NEW)
Block 3 - 1 byte (NEW) 
Block 4 - 256KB  (re-used)
Block 5 - 40KB   (re-used)
```

I think a better approach might be to instead store the update deltas also during checkpoint, so that we can checkpoint updates without having to re-write segments in their entirety, similar to how deletes are stored. Perhaps that approach could be considered as an alternative?
pr_title: Reuse unchanged persistent segments during checkpoint

body:
@Mytherin Thanks! Your alternative method makes sense to me. 

I also observed your concerns about sub-optimal compression. My current implementation uses heuristics (which is imperfect) to **detect fragmentation**. Whenever too much fragmentation is detected, it falls back to a full rewrite. Could this way of "conditioned full rewrite" be further polished or you see persisting update deltas as the preferred long-term direction?

body:
## Proposal

### Background

`StatisticsPropagator::TryExecuteAggregates` already replaces ungrouped `COUNT(*)` and plain-column `MIN`/`MAX` with constants when every partition has exact statistics. That rewrite is the aggregate-side counterpart of zonemap pruning: if the stored extrema already answer the query, there is no reason to scan the table.

Three limitations showed up while extending that path:

1. **The specialized byte-length fold needed a more general engine.** [#24967](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/24967) (discussion [#24966](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/24966)) folds `MIN`/`MAX(strlen)` / `MIN`/`MAX(octet_length)` from `min_string_length` / `max_string_length`. While implementing it, the same missing cases kept appearing for every aggregate family: all-NULL partitions, inexact min/max after deletes, filters that cut a row group, and functions of a column. Those belong in the fold engine, not in a strlen-only special case.

2. **All-NULL partitions and BOOLEAN were cheap, independent wins.** [#25621](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/25621) (still open; it is the first two commits of this branch) treats an all-NULL partition as neutral for `MIN`/`MAX`, and lets BOOLEAN use the numeric min/max statistics that it already stores.

3. **Inexact statistics do not have to mean "scan the table".** [#23611](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/23611) tries to *scan only the inexact partitions* and merge those results with the precomputed constants. [#24962](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/24962) then made that merge path unreachable. This branch does **not** revive that scan. It takes a different cut: if an inexact (or filter-cut) partition can only supply a bound, and that bound cannot beat the candidate already produced by exact partitions, the inexact partition can be dropped at plan time and the query still folds.


### What the branch does

#### 1. All-NULL partitions and BOOLEAN

Already opened as #25621.

- A partition that holds only NULL values cannot win `MIN`/`MAX`. It is now `NEUTRAL` instead of aborting the rewrite for the whole table.
- BOOLEAN already stores min/max in the numeric statistics, but `LogicalType::IsNumeric()` does not cover it. BOOLEAN is now folded like the other orderable numeric types.

#### 2. Extract a partition-fold engine

A behavior-preserving extraction of `TryExecuteAggregates`.

The ad-hoc MIN/MAX and `COUNT(*)` precompute becomes a compile-time `PartitionFold` client in `partition_fold.hpp`. Each aggregate family only says how one partition is classified and how values combine. Bail-path tests are locked in first so the extraction cannot silently change SUM, unsafe casts, LIMIT, sampling, generated columns, empty tables, CSV, truncated strings, or `STATE_EXPORT`. The unreachable scan-and-merge block that #24962 made dead is deleted rather than restored.

The four states the engine understands:

| State | Meaning | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EXACT_VALUE` | statistics name a real surviving row | becomes / updates the candidate |
| `BOUND` | statistics cover every surviving row, but are not attained | votes later; never becomes the candidate |
| `NEUTRAL` | partition contributes nothing (e.g. all-NULL for MIN/MAX) | ignored |
| `NO_INFO` | statistics do not describe the rows that will be read | the rewrite is abandoned |

A fold still requires at least one exact source. A bound alone never folds. `COUNT(*)` still requires an exact count: a filter-cut or approximate count is `NO_INFO`, not `BOUND`. Pending local writes are `NO_INFO` as well — those rows are not even covered by a bound.

#### 3. Bound voting

The inexact-stats cut, and it is plan-time only.

`BOUND` partitions vote instead of vetoing. After exact partitions have produced a candidate, each bound is dropped when it cannot change that candidate (`ExcludesCandidate`, weak domination: a tie is enough). If every bound is dominated, the rewrite folds and **no row group is scanned**. Filter-cut partitions use the same slot: a filter only removes rows, so the all-rows min/max remain a superset bound over the survivors. If every partition is filtered out, the aggregates fold to their empty-input results (`NULL` for MIN/MAX, `0` for `COUNT(*)`).

VARCHAR **value** bounds are not voted on: truncated 12-byte prefixes are not a safe upper bound. Empty-partition folding can replace a 0-row-group scan with a constant plan; both mean no data was read.

This PR never scans the inexact partitions. If a bound is not dominated, the whole rewrite is abandoned and execution proceeds as today. Bound voting is a complement, not a drop-in for partial precompute, and it does not reintroduce the row-group index problem.

#### 4. Two applications of the same engine

Once the engine exists, the original #24967 case and a monotone generalization become small clients.

**Byte length.** `MIN`/`MAX(strlen(VARCHAR))` and `MIN`/`MAX(octet_length(BLOB))` read `min_string_length` / `max_string_length`. Those length fields stay exact even when the string *value* statistics are truncated, so length bounds can vote. CSE-lifted `strlen(col)` projections are converted during the projection walk instead of disabling the rewrite. `octet_length(BIT)` is not recognized: BIT's stored size includes a padding byte. `length()` / `char_length()` still count code points and are left out.

**Monotone functions.** `MIN`/`MAX(f(col))` is recognized when `f` has `ArgProperties`, `FunctionStability::CONSISTENT`, exactly one column argument, and a numeric result. Both mapped endpoints are evaluated before folding (`TryEvaluateMonotoneEndpoints` → `TryEvaluateMonotoneCorners`, shared with `PropagateMonotoneBounds`). A decreasing function swaps the endpoints. Inexact or filter-cut partitions vote as `BOUND`. Functions that are not actually monotone over an arbitrary range have no annotation and do not fold. INTERVAL arguments are rejected because they are not totally ordered.
pr_title: Generalize eager MIN/MAX folding with partition bound voting

body:
Thanks for taking a look — agreed, buffering full copies of the inserted rows is not the right approach.                                  
                                                                                                                                  
The motivating case is #7168: rows referencing other rows of the same statement (e.g. a tree in a self-referencing table) fail today because validation runs per chunk, before the statement's own rows are visible.                                            
                                                                                                                                  
On rows referencing themselves: that's a side effect of deferring the check rather than the goal — at the end of the statement  such a row exists, so the constraint holds. Postgres seems to allow this as well. If you'd rather keep pure self-references an error, we can keep that with an explicit rule; please let me know which semantics you prefer.                                    
                                                                                                                                  
On avoiding the copy, two options:                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                  
(a) Buffer only the foreign key columns (projected per constraint) and verify against those at the end of the statement — memory proportional to keys, nothing re-read afterwards.                                                                                
                                                                                                                                  
(b) No buffer: track the row range this statement appended to the local storage and scan it at the end of the statement — flat memory, but large file-backed inserts may have spilled row groups to disk by then, requiring a read-back.                        
                                                                                                                                  
I'd prefer (a); happy to rework — or follow a different architecture if you have one in mind.

Hi — before updating this PR, I did a fresh audit against current `main` and found an important gap in the existing validation.

The added regression test sets `PRAGMA disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown` before the `restart` steps. That means it does not exercise the no-client-context shutdown-checkpoint path, and therefore does not prove that this PR's guard is reached. I should not treat the current test or validation as sufficient.

The underlying invariant from #23788 still holds on current `main`: an `UnboundIndex` with buffered WAL replays must not be serialized using only its pre-replay `IndexStorageInfo`, because that can persist an index missing recovered rows and lead to silent wrong results. Current `main` still has the corresponding no-context serialization FIXME.

There is also now relevant recovery support in #24260 for a failed checkpoint marker. That makes the design choice here more explicit:

* **A. Preflight/skip:** before `WALStartCheckpoint`, detect an unbound index with buffered replays when there is no client context, and skip this shutdown checkpoint without changing the WAL. A later context-bearing checkpoint can bind the index and persist it normally.
* **C. Fail closed after checkpoint start:** keep the current exception-based approach. This prevents corruption, but the checkpoint marker has already been written; the contract must explicitly cover invalidation/error handling during shutdown and recovery of the main/checkpoint WAL state on the next open.

I would appreciate maintainer guidance on which contract is preferred. Once that direction is clear, I will rebuild the change on current `main` and add an exact regression: two independent DuckDB engines in the same process, a pending WAL with a secondary ART index, the no-context checkpoint path, and a forced index-scan correctness check after reopening. If sqllogictest cannot model the two-engine setup, I will use the smallest appropriate C++ persistence/API test instead.
pr_title: Avoid corrupting buffered indexes during shutdown checkpoint

body:
I found a smaller, sequential three-process reproducer for the same stale secondary-index invariant. The manifestation is a deterministic `BoundIndex::Delete` fatal rather than a wrong-result index scan.

Environment: stock DuckDB CLI `v1.5.5 (Variegata) d8cdaa33fd`, Darwin arm64.

### Process 1: create a pending WAL and exit without a shutdown checkpoint

```sh
DB=/tmp/art_shutdown_checkpoint.db
rm -f "$DB" "$DB.wal" "$DB.wal.checkpoint" "$DB.wal.recovery"

duckdb "$DB" -c "
SET wal_autocheckpoint='1TB';
PRAGMA disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown;
CREATE TABLE t(
    serverid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    host VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    port INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX t_u01 ON t(host, port);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'host-a', 6432);
"

test -f "$DB.wal"
```

### Process 2: replay the WAL, do not touch the index, then exit

```sh
duckdb "$DB" -c "SELECT 1;"
test ! -e "$DB.wal"
```

The second process uses a fresh configuration, so `disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown` is no longer set. Opening replays the WAL into the lazy unbound secondary index; closing then runs the context-free shutdown checkpoint.

### Process 3: delete through the healthy primary key

```sh
duckdb "$DB" -c "DELETE FROM t WHERE serverid=1;"
```

Result:

```text
FATAL Error: Invalid Input Error: Failed to delete all rows from index. Only deleted 0 out of 1 rows.
Chunk: Chunk - [3 Columns]
- FLAT INTEGER: 1 = [ 1]
- FLAT VARCHAR: 1 = [ host-a]
- FLAT INTEGER: 1 = [ 6432]
```

The primary-key lookup still finds the table row, but removal from `t_u01` finds no corresponding entry. This is the same persisted table/index divergence viewed through the delete consistency check.

### Positive control

If Process 2 executes an explicit, context-bearing checkpoint instead:

```sh
duckdb "$DB" -c "CHECKPOINT;"
```

Process 3 succeeds and `SELECT count(*) FROM t` returns `0`. I reran the failing and control cases side by side against fresh files: failing shutdown path exited 1 with the fatal above; explicit-checkpoint control exited 0.

This supports option A from the latest discussion: preflight before `WALStartCheckpoint` and skip the context-free shutdown checkpoint while any unbound index has buffered replays. It also gives an exact oracle for the revised regression test. The test must reset the `disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown` setting between Process 1 and Process 2; an in-process `restart` that retains the setting will not reach this path.
pr_title: Avoid corrupting buffered indexes during shutdown checkpoint

body:
A third trigger for the same stale-secondary-index persistence, with the writer's exit being the realistic one: a writer process that dies **without closing its connection** (crash / SIGKILL / `process::exit` — no `disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown` needed), followed by any stock CLI open-and-exit.

**Environment:** DuckDB `v1.5.5 (Variegata) d8cdaa33fd` on both sides — the stock CLI and the `duckdb` Rust crate 1.10505.0 (bundled) — Linux 7.0.0 x86_64.

**Sequence** (single-threaded, one process at a time, never two engines on the file):

1. Writer (Rust crate): `INSERT` 30 rows into a table that has two secondary `CREATE INDEX`es (one DATE column, one BIGINT) inside `BEGIN … COMMIT`, then `std::process::exit(0)` without dropping the connection. The `.wal` is left pending. In-process before exit, index-served lookups on the new rows are correct.
2. `duckdb <file> </dev/null` — the CLI opens read-write and exits. No statement at all.
3. Reopen (either engine, read-only or read-write):
   - `SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE date_col = DATE '…'` → **0** (30 rows exist)
   - `SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE id_col = <max id>` → **0** (1 row exists)
   - `SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE date_col = DATE '…') FROM t` → 30 (scan-side, correct)
   - `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows the equality served by an index scan; `DROP INDEX` → 30.
   A second table written in the same step-1 transaction, with one secondary index on a VARCHAR column, lost its 30 entries in two of three runs.

**Controls, same pending WAL, each restores correctness:**
- step 2 done by the Rust crate instead (open, close cleanly) — fine;
- `duckdb -readonly <file>` — fine (cannot checkpoint; WAL stays);
- `duckdb <file> -c "CHECKPOINT"` — fine.

**One observation that matches #23848's root cause:** in a run where step 2 was `duckdb <file> -c "SELECT count(*) FROM t2 WHERE varchar_col = '…'"`, the index that query bound (t2's) was persisted correctly and the two unqueried indexes on t were not. With no statement, all three lost their entries. So it is per-index: whatever the CLI happened to bind before its context-free shutdown checkpoint survives; the rest is written from pre-WAL storage.

**Impact:** this reached a production file and stayed silent for five days — the writer service had been exiting without closing at every restart, and an unrelated `duckdb` CLI session on the file (opened read-write, exited normally) persisted the loss. Equality lookups on three tables returned wrong answers to application guards until an index-vs-scan consistency probe caught it. `DROP INDEX` + `CREATE INDEX` repaired it. The sequential form needs no concurrency and no special pragma, so it is reachable from any crashed writer plus a later CLI open.
pr_title: Avoid corrupting buffered indexes during shutdown checkpoint

The broader refactoring is very unlikely to land in 2.0, so I would not defer this regression on that basis. A targeted fix within the current architecture would still be useful.

My preference is to keep DELIM-to-CTE lowering in the planner and investigate whether we can improve filter propagation through the resulting CTEs. If that requires a substantially larger change, I'm open to a narrowly scoped extension of the existing pre-lowering pushdown as an interim solution.

body:
Thanks for continuing to work on this and for incorporating my feedback. After looking into it further, I think there is a more direct way to address the underlying problem.

When we rewrite the DELIM join into CTEs, we lose the information that the distinct correlation domain exists only to serve the outer rows. The CTE filter pusher then correctly treats both scans as independent consumers and cannot push the filter into their shared input. I think the better approach is to preserve that relationship during the rewrite, so the optimizer can use it without having to rediscover it through a more general analysis.

My concern with the current approach is that it adds substantial infrastructure and maintenance complexity to the CTE filter pusher for information we already have when constructing the plan. This should also be possible without waiting for the larger refactoring to remove DELIM joins, which is very unlikely to land in 2.0.

I'm going to take over the issue and pursue that approach. Given how closely this touches the decorrelation machinery, I think it makes sense for me to handle it. Thanks again for the investigation and the time you've put into this.
pr_title: Push filters through correlated joins before CTE lowering

body:
Thanks for investigating this and putting together a clear reproducer and regression tests. It's useful to see exactly where the current filter propagation stops working.

I do have concerns about the direction of the fix. My goal for this code is to remove DELIM joins entirely. Moving DELIM-to-CTE lowering into the optimizer lets us reuse the existing filter pushdown, but it also makes that optimization depend on keeping the DELIM representation around longer. That takes us away from the architecture I'm working towards.

The optimizer can also be disabled. I see that you've accounted for that with explicit lowering paths, but I'd prefer to keep lowering independent of optional optimization. We should still produce a correct CTE plan with optimization disabled, even if that plan is less efficient.

That doesn't necessarily mean this regression needs to wait for the full refactor. There may be a smaller fix that improves filter propagation through the generated CTEs while keeping lowering where it is. The complication is that the input CTE has multiple consumers, including the one that builds the distinct correlation keys, so we need to establish when restricting that input is safe. Extending the existing pre-lowering pushdown through ordinary joins is another possible interim fix, though it would add more specialized logic that we eventually want to remove.

Thank you for the review! 

Currently, the reason why we check per append is because this blob passing UINT32_MAX overflow can occur at any append, not  just the last one in a row.

Without the check at each step, once overflow occurs mid-row, the buffer will continue growing (which may not be significant for typical inputs, but larger inputs this means unnecessary expansion before the throw ever happens)

Happy to move to a single end-of-row check if that tradeoff isn't a

body:
You were right about the visible-before-durable part — a transaction starting while the fsync was still in flight could observe a commit that a crash would lose. I reworked that, and since the design ended up quite different from this PR, opened it separately rather than dumping it into this thread: #23655.

The gist: commit timestamps stay at commit time, but new snapshots are bounded at the durable horizon — a transaction that starts while a commit's fsync is pending simply doesn't see that commit yet. Same guarantee as assigning timestamps at publish time, but nothing blocks and publish order never changes, which is what keeps the patch small.

On "not as powerful": I ran your group_commit benchmark (extended with 2/32 threads and a 100ms latency tier) against both branches on a 32-core machine, numbers are in the PR. The main structural difference is that committers issue overlapping fsyncs instead of parking behind a single sync leader, which hides the fsync round trip on networked storage without needing a batching delay — whether fsyncs overlap or serialize is taken from the file system type rather than measured at runtime, and on local disks a single late-snapping fsync stream batches as well as a delay does. Appends do still serialize under the WAL lock, deliberately, since a page-cache append is orders of magnitude cheaper than the fsync it precedes.

One thing taken from this PR while reworking: the fsync-failure poisoning. The retry in the commit you looked at was indeed unsafe after a failed fsync, your handling is the correct one.

body:
This PR defers more than the fsync, it defers the **publish**. A commit's changes only become visible to other transactions after its flush marker is durable, otherwise a transaction could observe (and act on) a commit that a crash would lose. So while we wait for the fsync, the commit has deliberately *not* happened yet from the rest of the system's perspective.

The publish_gate then follows from what `transaction_lock` currently provides on main. There, a commit writes its WAL entries first (unvalidated, with the transaction lock released), and then, under `transaction_lock`, runs the conflict check (the `HasParent()` check in `CommitState::CommitEntry`: "has another transaction altered a table I modified?") and applies the consequences (version flips, index removal, becoming visible), entry by entry. A failed check reverts everything: the exclusively-held WAL is truncated and the applied entries are rolled back. DDL never takes `transaction_lock`; it doesn't need to, because a commit remains fully abortable until it completes. From DDL's perspective a commit is effectively a point event: `AlterEntry`'s new table version lands either early enough that a check catches it (clean abort) or after the commit is fully visible.

Deferring publish breaks the abortability that made this work: once a commit's flush marker is durable in a WAL that other commits keep appending to, it can neither be truncated nor rolled back (without bigger surgery and storage-related changes, e.g. a compensating abort record), so replay will apply it. The check must therefore move *before* the flush marker (out of the `transaction_lock` section, since the WAL write happens with `t_lock` released), while the consequences run *after* the fsync (back under `t_lock`, at publish). `t_lock` can't span the gap, as that would stall transaction start and all other commits for the duration of an fsync, which is the thing the feature exists to avoid. So there is now a window in which a commit has passed its checks, can no longer abort, and hasn't acted. An `ALTER TABLE t` landing inside it means the per-entry check in `CommitEntry` fires *past the point of no return*: the only remaining option is a fatal error, for what should be an ordinary transaction conflict (and I believe that failing the ALTER TABLE is not a viable option, DDL should not be sniped by DML).

The check also can't simply be skipped for deferred commits: the ALTER's rebuild and a `CREATE INDEX`'s attach would then proceed against a table state that excludes the pending commit. Concretely, a committed `UPDATE` on a retyped column gets lost (the rewrite bakes in the old value and the update lands on the discarded column), and a freshly attached index never receives the removals a publishing `DELETE` applies to every *attached* index, leaving a permanently untracked stale entry. The conflict is real; it just has to be resolved while aborting is still possible.

That's all the publish gate does: it pins the table state the validation saw until publish consumes it. It is the per-table replacement for the `transaction_lock` check/act piece. It can be seen as a **commit-scoped schema-stability lock**: commits hold it shared (they never block each other, so batching is unaffected; statements and reads never touch it), DDL on that table takes it exclusive for the duration of the catalog change. In the steady state it's uncontended; the only pairing that ever waits is a DDL vs. an in-flight commit on the same table, for at most about one fsync. It is the same pairing that on main resolves by aborting one side.

(Longer term I think the exclusive section can shrink to nearly nothing with a delta-catch-up ALTER — rebuild against a snapshot, apply the changes that committed meanwhile, swap under the gate for a final millisecond delta — which would also fix a family of existing rebuild races on main, e.g. rows committed between `CREATE INDEX`'s build scan and its attach are missing from the index today. That's a separate project though.)

**I think this is one of the key pieces of this work to discuss. If you agree with the direction, I can factor out this piece here as a first step. If you disagree, happy to discuss alternatives.**

I've went through the following options:

- **Compensating WAL abort records** (make post-marker abort possible): a WAL-format and replay change of its own magnitude, the abort record needs its own fsync before the failure can be reported, and reverting a commit a concurrent ALTER already rebuilt against reintroduces the structural races.
- **Fail or delay the DDL instead**: Implementing it requires atomically testing for in-flight commits and blocking new validations, which *is* the gate; waiting then preferred over failing (a busy table always has a commit in flight, and a fail-fast ALTER would hence starve).
- **Coarser locks**: holding `transaction_lock` across the fsync stalls transaction start and all commits; a global gate or having DDL take the WAL lock stalls *every* table's commits for the duration of an ALTER's table rewrite; reusing `append_lock` (a plain mutex) serializes same-table commits across the fsync, and reusing the per-table checkpoint lock creates a genuine deadlock cycle with the WAL lock ordering.
- **Delta-catch-up ALTER** (online-DDL style: rebuild against a snapshot, apply changes that committed meanwhile, swap under the gate for a final millisecond delta): the one genuine successor — it shrinks the exclusive publish gate section to nearly nothing *and* fixes a family of existing rebuild races on main (e.g. rows committed between `CREATE INDEX`'s build scan and its attach are missing from the index today). It's a separate, larger project.

So the publish gate (schema stability lock) felt like the best option.

I agree that it would be better if data that is not durable could not be read by other transactions - but I think the locking approach seems to introduce a lot of complexity.

Given the fact that we're MVCC anyway, perhaps an easier path is to have new transactions start at timestamps *prior* to any "committed-but-not-published" commits, e.g.:


```
COMMIT T1;     -- commits ts "2", not yet published
START T2;      -- starts at ts "1" (avoids reading committed but unpublished data)
PUBLISH T1;    -- now publish ts "2"
START T3;      -- starts at ts "2" since this transaction has been published
```

I feel that with this path we can avoid making any locking changes - all we need to do is start new transactions so that they can only see snapshots that have been both committed **and** published.

body:
Thanks — I checked #24919.

It covers grammar extension and context-free AST construction well. A grammar
transform can produce a regular DuckDB `SQLStatement`, so this PR would not be
needed for extensions whose lowering is independent of connection state.

The remaining case is context-dependent lowering. The grammar transform
currently receives `PEGTransformer &` and `ParseResult &`, but not the active
`ClientContext`. The existing `plan_function` does receive `ClientContext`, but
its result is restricted to a `TableFunction`, so it cannot lower the parsed
representation into a regular DuckDB statement that continues through the
normal binder and planner.

The capability needed here is therefore:

- parse extension syntax through `GrammarExtension`;
- retain an extension-owned parsed representation;
- lower it into exactly one regular `SQLStatement` with the active
  `ClientContext`, before binding.

I agree that this should not expand the legacy `ParserExtension` API. Would you
prefer this to be designed as an optional planner-time lowering callback
associated with `GrammarExtension`, or as a separate non-legacy extension API?

I am happy to rework this PR on top of #24919. @Tishj

body:
Thanks for the review! I've reworked the PR:

RowComparisonSimplificationRule now handles both sides uniformly — either side can be a row constructor (possibly wrapped in casts) or a folded TUPLE/STRUCT constant — and the comparison is unpacked into per-field scalar comparisons:

- Row-vs-row unpacks with IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, matching the row equality semantics
- Row-vs-constant with a NULL-free constant unpacks with =, which the filter combiner absorbs and pushes down as zone map filters
- Constants containing NULLs unpack with IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (e.g. (a, b) = (NULL, 2) matches rows with a IS NULL), which = cannot express

The CI failures appear to be network-related flakes.

body:
Thanks - I reworked it along those lines, and updated the description with the details.

One thing I ran into: I first tried the separate rule that rewrites `x IS NOT DISTINCT FROM <non-NULL constant>`
to `x = <constant>` at the root of a filter. For `AND(x IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 1, y IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 2)` the
conjuncts are not really "at the root" - the filter splits the AND, puts the first conjunct back where the AND
used to be and never looks at it again, so a root-only rule only ends up rewriting some of them. Matching the AND
as well would work, but it felt less clean.

Then I remembered I already have #24605 open, which teaches the filter combiner to accept IS NOT DISTINCT FROM
(a non-NULL constant folds to equality, NDF pairs are tracked so NULL semantics do not change). That covers the
second half, so this PR can stay a plain unpacking rule - and on its own it still fixes the issue.

I think this split might be a bit cleaner.

Adapting to out of band comments, some changes:

1. `REGISTER` to be the verb to register an internal name for a given resource
2. `CONNECT TO NEW TEMPORARY EXTERNAL RESOURCE` for making explicit an ephemeral resource is created
3. `FROM duckdb_external_resources(discover:=true)` to be the table function, so to be able to filter and all

There is not yet a single statement way to go from an handle to using (or deleting an handle). Currently flow would be:
```sql
--- get the handle
SET VARIABLE machine_handle = (SELECT handle FROM duckdb_external_resources(discover := true) LIMIT 1);

---register to a name
REGISTER EXTERNAL RESOURCE '<type>' AS resource_name FROM $machine_handle;

--- use, for example, delete:
DESTROY EXTERNAL RESOURCE resource_name;
```
given registration an use are in most cases tied 1 to 1, it would be great to fuse them into a single:
```
DESTROY EXTERNAL RESOURCE $machine_handle;
--- or
DESTROY EXTERNAL RESOURCE FROM $machine_handle;
```
This is not part of the PR.

Thanks!!

Codex also found the following issue: 
The existing test only checks the exact read_only spelling returned by
ro_status. AttachOptions also interprets readonly, readwrite, and read_write as
the same underlying access_mode setting, but the collision check compares
textual keys.

Could we add regression coverage for both the spelling alias and the wider
semantic collision? The first new case currently succeeds unexpectedly,
confirming the bypass.

```
diff --git a/test/sql/attach/external_resource_option_collision.test b/test/sql/attach/external_resource_option_collision.test
index 725b08b01e..27e478a4d6 100644

@@ -47,6 +47,18 @@ ATTACH TO EXTERNAL RESOURCE pinned_ro AS b1 (READ_ONLY 1);
 ----
 <REGEX>:.*the resource supplies "read_only".*

+# ro_status supplies read_only=true; READONLY is an alternate spelling of that
```

I think these rules have quite some overlap and can be simplified, so its easier to spot the difference between the two. Also there's two `AttachOptions` which seem confusing, so I'd rename one to `ExternalResourceOptions`, same with `ExternalResourceAlias`. Overall the grammar becomes a bit more verbose, but easier to understand in my opinion of what piece does what. 
```
WithExternalResourceStatement <- 'WITH' 'EXTERNAL' 'RESOURCE'
    Expression ExternalResourceAlias? ExternalResourceOptions?
    WithExternalResourceAction AttachOptions?

WithExternalResourceAction <-
    WithExternalResourceAttach / WithExternalResourceConnect

WithExternalResourceAttach <- 'ATTACH' AttachAlias?
WithExternalResourceConnect <- 'CONNECT'

ExternalResourceAlias <- AttachAlias
ExternalResourceOptions <- AttachOptions
```

body:
> Exciting stuff!
> 
> I started reading the description, and I think it could use some polish The initial example for error handling is incorrect.
> 
> * message_view -> msg
> * duckdb_v2_error_i -> ???
>
> Also, bit of a nitpick since it is just an example, but in your example the destroying of the error is unnecessary since it exits the process anyway. The destroy would be only be required if the process were meant to continue.

Good points, will adjust!

> > Note that the last duckdb_v2_error_info_handle argument is always optional, and will only be set if an error actually occurred. So you only have to check the returned error code if you don't care about additional error details.
> 
> This is slightly misleading I think? You need to check it if you set the `duckdb_v2_error_info_handle` reference (pass a non-null pointer), because that indicates intent, and causes an allocation of the handle, right?

You can't create your own duckdb_v2_error_info_hande, so you can't really pass a non-null pointer (or well a pointer to a non-null pointer) unless you already had a previous error (which you should deal with it).
The whole point is that we _dont_ allocate in the success-path, so there is no error info to free. But you can also just call duckdb_v2_error_info_destroy unconditionally as passing a pointer-to-null to destructors is safe.

> #### `duckdb_v2_str`
> "extend its lifetime" What exactly is the lifetime guarantee of a duckdb-owned str? Is this annotated on the returning function or is this implicit only? I think this needs more consideration if its only implicit. My initial thought was adding a `const char* lifetime;` to the struct, to annotate with predefined constants like "environment", "database", "connection". ^ that could also be a `void *owning_handle;`, set to the handle who's lifetime its connected to. Ignore this comment if there's already a good convention in place, then I'd just like to see it in the description 👍
> 
> EDIT: I went through the PR afterwards, looks like it's annotated on the returning function. I'm still a little worried about future methods that might have a dynamic owner of returned string data (i.e multiple handles are involved, memory could belong to either one).

This is more of a theoretical concern than a practical one, I could make the same argument agains passing a `const char*`. The convention we use in this API: that `duckdb_v2_str` is always borrowed is strictly better as it's at least consistent, compared to the V1-API where you sometimes owned and had to free return char* pointers, and sometimes not. 

As of now we don't return dynamic strings as duckdb_v2_str's at all, and I don't think we really want to anyway as you would have to cache it somewhere on a handle (and indeed start thinking about the lifetime/validity of the pointer now). The few places we want to be able to pass dynamically constructed strings we instead use a callback-based approach to make it clear that the string you receive is alive within a transient scope (the duration of the callback). I think callbacks are superior anyway as we could then also look into essentially "streaming" large strings by just repeatedly invoking the user supplied callback with the next part of the string too.

> #### Statement expansion
> Have we not considered separating binding from execution? That could bite us later, no?

We have, its not part of this PR, but there is a `duckdb_v2_prepared_statement` in the fork.

> > Statements are parsed lazily, meaning that you can e.g. load a parser extension, and then use the new syntax immediately in the same SQL string.
> 
> I'd hold off on that, because currently the plan for both parser extension types is to require manually enabling them. And with dialect extensions there's another caviat because the entire query gets tokenized in its entirety before parsing further. We might still fix that before 2.0, but maybe not.

I think you've misunderstood, the lazy iteration is exactly what allows you to "manually enable" e.g. syntax extensions. You can pass `"LOAD my_ext; SET enable_special_syntax; SELECT foo WITH MY SYNTAX"` as one query, which will get expanded into three separate statements, which you can execute sequentially.

I don't know enough about dialect extensions to comment on that. Either way this design was not chosen specifically for parser extensions, but rather by the fact that having users manually split statements by looking for ";" by themselves, or not being able to distinguish if a query result came from a separate statement within the same query string, is very error prone.

I think at the end both a bound on Transformer AND a check at the start of the Binder (or, as here, at the boundary) are both handy to have, and I don't see how one replaces the other.

I didn't articulate clearly, the goal is not changing the unittest itself, that works fine as is, but allow multiple instance of the unittest to work side-by-side for an extension that would allow to do:
```sql
INSTALL AND LOAD sqllogictest;
.timer on
FROM run_tests('test/sql/types/uuid/');  --- run locally available tests
```
```
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬───────────────────┬───────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
     │                                                   name                                                   │ status  │ message │ statements_passed │ statements_failed │ statements_skipped │ assertions │ duration_ms │
     │                                                 varchar                                                  │ varchar │ varchar │      uint64       │      uint64       │       uint64       │   uint64   │   double    │
     ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼───────────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
     │ ./test/sql/types/uuid/test_uuid.test_slow          │ SUCCESS │ NULL    │                45 │                 0 │                  0 │        123 │  172.118167 │
     │ ./test/sql/types/uuid/test_uuid_cast.test          │ SUCCESS │ NULL    │                10 │                 0 │                  0 │         10 │    7.279583 │
     │ ./test/sql/types/uuid/test_uuid_uhugeint_cast.test │ SUCCESS │ NULL    │                12 │                 0 │                  0 │         12 │    9.148584 │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴───────────────────┴───────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘
     Run Time (s): real 0.207 user 0.132500 sys 0.030221
```

This PR in particular would allow to bolt parallelism on top:
```sql
FROM run_tests('test/sql/types/');  --- run locally available tests, 464 of them
--- 18.29s (single sample, there is randomness)
FROM run_tests('test/sql/types/', workers:=8);  --- run locally available tests, 464 of them, up to 8 at a time
--- 4.85 (single sample, there is randomness, but some parallelism kicks in)
```

If you want to give a review in particular to https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/25489/changes/2954415f861199fd174a99641133b8339b8b19a7, that's the commit that deals with parallelism, very welcome.

body:
I would like this PR to add a dedicated benchmark before merging. The existing tiny-frontier benchmark has no invariant build, so it cannot protect this improvement. Specifically, I want the following synthetic two-hop traversal, with edge generation in the benchmark's **load phase**:

```sql
CREATE TABLE edges AS
SELECT
    (i // 10)::BIGINT AS src,
    (((i // 10) * 13 + i % 10 + 7) % 2000000)::BIGINT AS dst
FROM range(20000000) AS t(i);
```

Only this query should be timed:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE bidirectional_edges AS (
    SELECT src, dst FROM edges
    UNION ALL
    SELECT dst AS src, src AS dst
    FROM edges
    WHERE src <> dst
), walk(node, depth) AS (
    SELECT 65504::BIGINT, 0
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.dst, w.depth + 1
    FROM walk w
    JOIN bidirectional_edges e ON e.src = w.node
    WHERE w.depth < 2
)
SELECT depth, count(*) AS paths, sum(node) AS checksum
FROM walk
GROUP BY depth
ORDER BY depth;
```

The expected-answer file should contain:

```text
depth|paths|checksum
0|1|65504
1|20|16719860
2|400|310599200
```

Please leave the thread count configurable so we can exercise both the single-thread fallback and the parallel build. I validated this benchmark with one warmup and five measured runs per revision: at eight threads, the median improved from **330 ms to 121 ms** on an M5 Max.

I would also add a smaller regression test checking that the build is retained exactly once, `workers_max` remains 1, and `max_pipeline_workers` follows the configured thread count. That protects the scheduling decision directly, alongside the benchmark protecting its performance.
pr_title: Parallelize invariant recursive builds with small frontiers

I'm not sure this is the correct behavior, here's my thoughts
- `MOVEFILE_COPY_ALLOWED` flag is used to copy cross volume (see https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-movefileexa); current behavior matches unix one, `EXDEV` error will be returned when cross mounted filesystem be requested (see https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html)
- Current implementation in v2.0 seems to [have the same behavior](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/714b5904e607eecf40ce5abcc21e308c34ad4142/src/common/local_file_system.cpp#L1608)
- It doesn't provide atomicity (it's basically copy + delete operation involve data replication), which is required and often assumed by WAL write
- If we have certain feature requested in the future, I'm thinking to have another API to provide cross-volume move without atomicity guarantee

This exposes the missing `TIME -> TIME_NS` cast in `src/function/cast/time_casts.cpp`.

A multi-file scan combining `TIME(MICROS)` and `TIME(NANOS)`:
  - Errors with `union_by_name=true`.
  - Errors when the nanos file defines the default schema.
  - Succeeds but rounds away nanoseconds when the micros file defines the schema.

Repro:
```sql
require parquet

statement ok
COPY (SELECT '12:34:56.123456'::TIME AS t)
TO '{TEST_DIR}/time_micro.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);

statement ok
COPY (SELECT '12:34:56.123456789'::TIME_NS AS t)
TO '{TEST_DIR}/time_nano.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET);

query TT rowsort
SELECT typeof(t), t::VARCHAR
FROM read_parquet(['{TEST_DIR}/time_micro.parquet', '{TEST_DIR}/time_nano.parquet'], union_by_name = true);
----
TIME_NS	12:34:56.123456
TIME_NS	12:34:56.123456789
```

Evaluating expressions before or after joins seems like an interesting avenue for optimization - but the decision seems complex to make:

1. **`alias()` can change results after export.**

   ```sql
   SELECT alias(i) AS renamed FROM (VALUES (1), (2)) t(i);
   ```

body: For normal SQL binding the catalog entry is transaction-visible. The distinction matters because these `FunctionBinder` overloads are public and accept a catalog-entry reference directly. That reference does not necessarily come from a lookup in this `ClientContext`. For example, callers can construct a `ScalarFunctionCatalogEntry` or `AggregateFunctionCatalogEntry` against a real catalog/schema without registering it. It can have the same qualified name and can even contain the actual live overload pointer, but it is still not the catalog entry visible through this transaction. An older entry version after replacement/drop, or an entry obtained under another transaction snapshot, has the same issue. The check therefore looks the entry up by type/name in the current transaction and requires object identity with the supplied entry. Without that check, passing a forged or stale entry through the public catalog-entry binder would be enough to attach an authenticated recipe.
pr_title: Add structural SQL export for bound expressions

body:
There are two separate points here. This condition is not "the function changed, so remember the original." It verifies that the selected overload came from this exact transaction-visible catalog entry and that binding still identifies that overload as its canonical definition. Binding may specialize the current execution implementation, but that specialization is not what grants the recipe.

The definition plus argument expressions are not sufficient because they do not authenticate the expression occurrence. `BoundScalarFunction` and `BoundAggregateFunction` are copyable and retain their definition pointers. A caller can copy an authenticated bound function, change its name or callbacks, and construct a new public bound expression with the same children. For a name-sensitive function, that expression can e.g. execute as `8` while SQL reconstructed from the retained definition binds and executes as `7`. A live definition pointer can likewise be placed in a forged/non-visible catalog entry.

The recipe is the expression-owned provenance marker that distinguishes those cases. Copying the complete expression preserves it. Copying a function or using a public constructor does not. Broad mutation consumes it, while the narrow execution-only specialization APIs preserve it under the optimizer's semantic-equivalence contract. The argument ASTs are not duplicated in the recipe, only the authenticated logical name/signature is kept separately from the current execution implementation.
pr_title: Add structural SQL export for bound expressions

body:
I agree that function pointers are not a stable function identity. They are not intended to be used as identity here. The qualified name and signature identify the logical SQL function, while the callback pointers only select how that function executes inside the current DuckDB process.

This separate type is needed because `ReplaceImplementation` changes the whole function, including its name, return type, properties, bind callbacks, and serialization callbacks. E.g. for the `sum` optimization, we only want to replace the execution callbacks with those from `sum_no_overflow`, while the expression remains logically `sum`. The pointer comparisons are only used in the test to confirm that the local optimization happened.

body:
@hawkfish to get back on this in a little more detail, the query I used was:

```sql
ROWS BETWEEN mod(b * 47, 521) PRECEDING
         AND 100 - mod(b * 47, 521) FOLLOWING
```

This resulted in roughly the same performance, but to get a better view I also ran some other queries (generated by codex) which trigger the MST path. I'm not sure how representative they are for real-world workloads however:

### Significant overlap with periodic jump

```sql
CREATE TABLE rank_mst AS
SELECT
    b % 100 AS a,
    b,
    mod(b * 2, 521) AS p
FROM range(10000000) tbl(b);

SELECT sum(m)
FROM (
    SELECT mad(a) OVER (
        ORDER BY b
        ROWS BETWEEN p PRECEDING
                 AND 100 - p FOLLOWING
    ) AS m
    FROM rank_mst
) q;
```

### Long slides with significant overlap separated by jumps

```sql
CREATE TABLE rank_mst_blocks AS
SELECT
    b % 100 AS a,
    b,
    CASE WHEN (b // 1024) % 2 = 0 THEN 0 ELSE 500 END AS p
FROM range(10000000) tbl(b);

SELECT sum(m)
FROM (
    SELECT mad(a) OVER (
        ORDER BY b
        ROWS BETWEEN p PRECEDING
                 AND 100 - p FOLLOWING
    ) AS m
    FROM rank_mst_blocks
) q;
```

### Almost no overlap

```sql
CREATE TABLE rank_mst_alternating AS
SELECT
    b % 100 AS a,
    b,
    CASE WHEN b % 2 = 0 THEN 0 ELSE 100 END AS p
FROM range(10000000) tbl(b);

SELECT sum(m)
FROM (
    SELECT mad(a) OVER (
        ORDER BY b
        ROWS BETWEEN p PRECEDING
                 AND 100 - p FOLLOWING
    ) AS m
    FROM rank_mst_alternating
) q;
```

### Slowly expanding frame

```sql
CREATE TABLE rank_mst_width AS
SELECT
    b % 500 AS a,
    b,
    mod(b, 501) AS p
FROM range(10000000) tbl(b);

SELECT sum(m)
FROM (
    SELECT mad(a) OVER (
        ORDER BY b
        ROWS BETWEEN p PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS m
    FROM rank_mst_width
) q;
```

### Two subframes

```sql
CREATE TABLE rank_mst_exclude AS
SELECT
    b % 500 AS a,
    b,
    mod(b, 501) AS p
FROM range(10000000) tbl(b);

SELECT sum(m)
FROM (
    SELECT mad(a) OVER (
        ORDER BY b
        ROWS BETWEEN p PRECEDING AND p FOLLOWING
        EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW
    ) AS m
    FROM rank_mst_exclude
) q;
```

## Results

MST frame behavior | Baseline | PR | Improvement
-- | -- | -- | --
Significant overlap with periodic jump | 17.460s | 10.236s | 41.4%
Long slides with significant overlap separated by jumps | 11.551s | 9.981s | 13.6%
Almost no overlap | 27.005s | 10.008s | 62.9%
Slowly expanding frame | 75.527s | 24.116s | 68.1%
Two subframes | 33.141s | 3.944s | 88.1%

Just to confirm and clarify the distinction, however, I want to confirm that is is ok to copy out a NodePtr "value" in a lot of scenarios (for example lookup, stack based traversal) whereas what was unsafe before was copying out the _references_ to NodePtrs, not the NodePtrs themselves. 

E.g. a reference to a NodePtr presupposes some stable memory for where the NodePtr is resident, which is the unsafe part. Whereas the NodePtr is just 64 bits referring to a stable node entity in the ART that we can always re-pin if we need to get the node into memory.

body:
Thanks for the PR! A few comments:

1. `TryReadSuffix` and the metadata used to validate/cache the returned bytes need to represent the same snapshot. Currently the suffix bytes and file size are obtained first, and `InitializeFileMetadata` fetches the version information afterwards. If the file changes in between, we can cache old bytes under the new metadata. Could we return the relevant metadata as part of `SuffixReadResult`, or otherwise make this a single snapshot?

2. `disable_parquet_prefetching` is currently bypassed by the suffix path, since it always requests `MAX_PREFETCH_SIZE`. Could we request only the final 8 bytes when prefetching is disabled? The external file cache can still apply its normal block caching policy.

3. I would copy the final cache block into a regular cache buffer and keep the existing invariant that cached data starts at offset zero. Avoiding this one `memcpy` adds `buffer_offset` handling to reads, debug verification, and reindexing. Could we remove `buffer_offset` and the nullable `owned_suffix` mode from `TryCacheSuffixBlock`?

4. A few smaller cleanups: the multi-state combinations of `needs_reopen`/`needs_metadata_refresh` and `suffix_read`/`file_proto` would be clearer as enums or helper results. The `TryReadSuffix` return value itself is fine as a `bool`. Also, `CreateThriftMemoryProtocol` can accept `data_ptr_t` to avoid the `const_cast`, and `SuffixReadResult::start_offset` appears redundant with `file_size - bytes_read`.

pr_title: Export re2 symbols

body:
We use DuckDB as a shared library (`libduckdb.so`) in our tests and want to use `duckdb_re2` in both test and production code. However, RE2's symbol visibility is set to "hidden" in `duckdb/third_party/re2/CMakeLists.txt:16`, which prevents RE2 symbols from being exported from the shared library.

When our test code attempts to construct an RE2 object, the linker cannot find the RE2 constructor in `libduckdb.so` due to hidden symbols. As a result, the linker statically compiles a second, complete copy of the RE2 implementation directly into our test/production binaries.

This creates **two separate instances** of RE2's global state (`empty_storage`):
1. One inside `libduckdb.so`
2. One inside our test/production binary

**This a problem** because RE2 maintains a global static variable:
```cpp
alignas(EmptyStorage) static char empty_storage[sizeof(EmptyStorage)];
```

We then crash when an RE2 object is constructed using one copy of `empty_storage` but destroyed using the other. The pointer comparison `error_arg_ != empty_string()` compares against the *wrong* copy of `empty_storage` (`empty_string()` is backed by `empty_storage`), causing the check to incorrectly succeed. This attempts to `delete` an unallocated `error_arg_`, resulting in a SIGSEGV in jemalloc (stacktrace below).

```cpp
if (error_arg_ != empty_string())
    delete error_arg_;
```

```
#0  atomic_load_p (a=0xd7a68, mo=atomic_memory_order_relaxed) at /server/duckdb/extension/jemalloc/jemalloc/include/jemalloc/internal/atomic.h:85
#1  rtree_leaf_elm_bits_read (elm=0xd7a68, dependent=true, tsdn=<optimized out>, rtree=<optimized out>) at /server/duckdb/extension/jemalloc/jemalloc/include/jemalloc/internal/rtree.h:185
#2  rtree_leaf_elm_read (elm=0xd7a68, dependent=true, tsdn=<optimized out>, rtree=<optimized out>) at /server/duckdb/extension/jemalloc/jemalloc/include/jemalloc/internal/rtree.h:247
```

body:
```suggestion
	const uint64_t retry_backoff_base_ms;
```
since it doesn't mean the overall retry timeout, but a base value.

I'm wondering do you think it's better to cap total retry attempt time duration? 
My take
- Nested retry attempts itself is not evil, having multiplication of retries is not easy to avoid in some cases, for example, 3rd party lib could have its own retry logic (don't think it's the case for DuckDB), sub-request (i.e., write operation splits into initiate + multiple part upload + finalization), etc.
- The goal, I assume, is to avoid indefinite retries across multiple layers. I think as long as all retry attempts follow exponential retry policy, and the operation overall is capped by a timeout, it should be good.

golang's [`context`](https://pkg.go.dev/context) design is used across their IO system, you could tell it adopts the similar philosophy:
- A centralized "token" (or "budged" in this PR), which passes down across all layers
- The `context` itself carries operation timeout information (instead of a retry count)

Updated according to latest iteration. Also rewritten the PR description, in particular left as follow ups the following:

Known limitations, both addressable as follow-ups:
- a pid identifies a process only within one PID namespace on one host. A temp_directory shared across containers, or over NFS between hosts, can hold files whose owner is alive elsewhere but absent locally. A potential follow-up is a policy file in the directory — an unknown policy means "only clean up after yourself" — which then lets a host/namespace key be introduced as a new policy value without older versions destroying files they cannot reason about; That would also avoid checking for PID, allowing an escape hatch if that code were to be off
- files left by a crash are now reclaimed when something next spills into that directory, where before they were wiped by the next instance's teardown. Since that wipe is exactly the behaviour being removed, the trade is deliberate, and a CALL cleanup_temporary_directory() is the natural follow-up for reclaiming on demand


I have NOT added UUID generation as part of this PR, was in https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/24655, I think that is orthogonal and can revive independently.

body:
I checked the ordering between transaction commit and the statistics updates, and merging the transaction-local statistics is both correct and strictly better than dropping them. `LocalStorage` is per-transaction, so we only ever merge our own uncommitted writes; and the committed stats are merged at commit time under the same lock readers use, before the transaction is published to new snapshots. So for any snapshot, the stats can only over-approximate the nullability of the rows it sees. That means `has_null` is never spuriously false, which is exactly what keeps the `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM → =` rewrite safe.
I think dropping the statistics instead would be less ideal, since it would give up the stats for the rest of the transaction even when the local writes contain no NULLs.

Hi Sander, thanks for your comments!

> @staticlibs i made a PR to detect these stack overflows in linux release tests under glibc by reducing the worker thread's stack size (similar size as musl).

I think the linked PR is really only tangentially related to this one (by touching the same options). The intention of this PR is to "have it [musl] closer in behaviour to glibc", thus making the playing field level for both glibc and musl.

> We can increase the worker thread's stack size with the linker flag, but that would increase duckdb's memory usage for all musl builds, right?

No, the Resident Set Size is expected to stay the same.

body:
Thanks for the PR!

The speed-ups are very promising, but implementation-wise this is very bolted-on and hard-coded only for filters. In general we've been trying to unify filters with expression execution, because there is no reason for filters to be anything but expression execution, and by moving optimizations into expression execution everything benefits and not just filters that are pushed down into table scans. This moves back in the other direction again by special casing implementation code for filters only. 

Two different implementation approaches I could see:

* Allow `SelectionVector` to be *either* a bitmap *or* a set of indices, where if you access it using certain APIs (e.g. `.data()` or `.get_index`) a transformation to the "standard" selection vector will be forced similar to what is going on in this API. Code can then take advantage of bitmap selection vectors where performance is desired.
* Add a new vector type to model "bitmap selection over a vector", separate from `DICTIONARY_VECTOR`, then take advantage of that vector type in certain code paths.

I think integrating this into the `SelectionVector` is the most promising. We can then proceed with integrating this into the expression execution layer (instead of the filter layer directly).
pr_title: autovec-friendly logic

body:
Thanks Mark — I integrated the bitmap representation into the SelectionVector.
- I added a subclass SelectionResult of SelectionVector (private inheritance): the subclass backs its selection with either an index array or a bitmap (SelectionData gained the bitmap buffer + row span); the base class is always a sel_t array. Existing code calls selvec.get_index(i) in performance-critical loops and must never bump into a bitmap — private inheritance makes that a compile-time guarantee: a SelectionResult can only cross into SelectionVector land through an explicit Flattened(), a once-per-vector materialization.
-  The branchless comparison kernels live in the expression Select layer and emit a bitmap whenever the caller's output selection is a SelectionResult (bitmap-aware consumers then intersect directly, e.g. conjunction AND). So the operator opts in, by declaring its result a SelectionResult — this is helpful because  producing bitmap output always regresses in operators that immediately need indices.

Net effect is less filter-specific code, with the fast path living where all selection happens. I did try first with all in SelectionVector, but  would have had to call Flatten() on it in many code locations, which is error-prone. Existing extension code that uses SelectionVector can safely continue to use it without danger of bumping into a bitmap.

Happy to iterate on the SelectionVector API shape if you'd like it drawn differently.

I also decided to **delete fastpfor** (from Daniel Lemire) introducing an own implementation because it is faster:
- a completely **generic** C++ templated naive [un]pack is faster because fastpfor compiled into 32 C methods that yielded 8,16,32 tuples (depending on width). This meant that the C function had to be called many times for e.g. 1024 tuples in a segment: call overhead and lost compiler optimization opportunities. Auto-vectorization and templating support in compiler got better in the years since fastpfor was created, favoring plain C++.
- a **shuffle** variant for certain bitwidths with clang/gcc. SIMD can help a lot (alas DuckDB does not use _interleaved_ bitpacking, then this would fly) but even with the sequential bit-layout used in DuckDB, one can take advantage of byte-shuffle instructions to assemble a destination lane, by putting input bytes there, and then doing shift and mask.

The new autovec codepaths are disabled in DUCKDB_SMALL_BINARY to keep code size down there.
They are taken by clang/gcc compiled ARM targets and x86 if they support AVX2 (a   runtime condition there), but are avoided on other platforms (those presumably without any good SIMD support).

Thanks for the detailed repro — that's convincing. I had assumed temp_directory was effectively single-owner, but your example clearly shows concurrent sharing is a supported use case today, so my current approach isn't safe.

One direction I was considering is using file locking instead of filename matching alone. DuckDB already has `FileLockType` (e.g. `READ_LOCK`/`WRITE_LOCK`) in the filesystem layer. Would it make sense to attempt acquiring an exclusive lock on each `duckdb_temp_*` file before deleting it, only removing files where the lock succeeds and skipping files that are still in use by another process?

Another idea that occurred to me is giving each active DuckDB instance its own subdirectory (or another form of per-instance ownership) under `temp_directory`, so cleanup becomes scoped to that instance instead of scanning a shared namespace. That feels simpler architecturally, but it would obviously be a larger behavioral change.

Or is there a different ownership/recovery mechanism you'd prefer for this? I'd rather align with the intended design than head off in the wrong direction.
